topics.title: Cell Structure & Organisation
topics.description: The cell as the unit of life, its internal structure, and how cells combine into tissues, organs and systems.

subtopics.title: Cell Theory & Discovery of the Cell

stories.sub: Why do we call it a ‘cell’?
stories.heading: A word borrowed from monks' rooms
list: Robert Hooke examined a thin slice of cork bark under a primitive microscope in 1665.
He saw tiny box-like compartments and thought they resembled the small rooms (‘cellulae’) monks lived in.
He named them ‘cells’ — the word has stuck for over 350 years.
What he actually saw were dead plant cell walls, not living cells — living cells weren't properly described until later.
stories.narration: In 1665, Robert Hooke looked at cork bark under a microscope and saw tiny box-like compartments. They reminded him of the small rooms monks lived in, called cellulae, so he named them cells. The word has stuck for over three hundred and fifty years, even though what he actually saw were dead plant cell walls, not living cells.

stories.sub: One idea, three scientists, seventeen years
stories.heading: How Cell Theory came together
list: Matthias Schleiden (1838) studied plants and concluded all plant tissue is made of cells.
Theodor Schwann (1839) extended this to animals: all animals are made of cells too.
Rudolf Virchow (1855) added the missing piece: ‘Omnis cellula e cellula’ — every cell comes from a pre-existing cell.
Together, these three statements became the Cell Theory you're tested on today.
stories.narration: Between 1838 and 1855, three scientists built Cell Theory piece by piece. Schleiden showed all plants are made of cells. Schwann showed all animals are made of cells too. And Virchow added the final rule: every cell comes from a cell that already existed.

lessons.heading: What is a cell?
list: A cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life.
Every living thing — bacterium, mushroom, oak tree, elephant, you — is built from cells.
Some organisms are just one cell (unicellular); others are trillions of cells working together (multicellular).
lessons.sub: Think of a cell as the smallest ‘brick’ that is still alive on its own.
lessons.narration: A cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life. Every living thing is built from cells — some organisms are just one cell, others are made of trillions working together.

lessons.heading: The three laws of Cell Theory
list: 1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in organisms.
3. All cells arise from pre-existing cells, by cell division.
lessons.sub: WAEC loves to test these three statements word-for-word — learn them exactly.
lessons.narration: Cell Theory has three parts. All living organisms are made of one or more cells. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function. And all cells arise from pre-existing cells by division.

lessons.heading: Light microscope vs electron microscope
list: Light microscope: uses light and glass lenses; magnifies up to about ×1500; can view living cells.
Electron microscope: uses a beam of electrons; magnifies over ×500,000; shows fine organelle detail; cannot view living cells.
Magnification is how much bigger an image looks; resolution is how clearly two close points can be told apart.
lessons.sub: A microscope can magnify a blur bigger without improving resolution — that's why resolution matters more.
lessons.narration: A light microscope uses light and glass lenses and can view living cells, but only magnifies up to about fifteen hundred times. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, magnifies over five hundred thousand times, but cannot view living cells.

lessons.heading: Surface area to volume ratio
list: As a cell grows bigger, its volume increases faster than its surface area.
A large cell would struggle to exchange enough oxygen, nutrients and waste across its surface fast enough to serve all that volume.
This is a major reason cells stay microscopically small.
lessons.sub: Small cells = more surface area per unit volume = faster exchange with the environment.
lessons.narration: As a cell grows bigger, its volume increases faster than its surface area. A large cell would struggle to exchange enough oxygen, nutrients and waste across its surface — which is a major reason cells stay microscopically small.

lessons.heading: Unicellular vs multicellular organisms
list: Unicellular organisms (e.g. Amoeba, bacteria, Paramecium) are made of just one cell that carries out every life process alone.
Multicellular organisms (e.g. humans, plants, mushrooms) are made of many cells that specialise and cooperate.
Specialisation lets multicellular organisms grow larger and more complex than any single cell could manage alone.
lessons.sub: One cell doing everything, versus many cells each doing one job well.
lessons.narration: Unicellular organisms are made of just one cell that does everything. Multicellular organisms are made of many cells that specialise and cooperate, letting them grow larger and more complex.

lessons.heading: Common WAEC pitfalls on Cell Theory
list: Do not say Hooke discovered living cells — he only saw dead cork cell walls.
Do not merge the three cell theory statements into one vague sentence; WAEC often asks you to state them separately.
Viruses are NOT made of cells, so strictly they fall outside the ‘all organisms are made of cells’ statement — a favourite trick question.
lessons.sub: Read past questions carefully: WAEC often asks which statement is NOT part of the cell theory.
lessons.narration: Common WAEC pitfalls: don't say Hooke discovered living cells — he only saw dead cork walls. Don't merge the three cell theory statements into one vague sentence. And remember, viruses are not made of cells.

quiz.question: According to Cell Theory, where do new cells come from?
options: They form spontaneously from non-living matter
They are created only inside the nucleolus
They only arise in multicellular organisms
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Virchow's principle: every cell comes from a cell that already existed.
quiz.explainWrong: Cell Theory states new cells arise only from pre-existing cells by division, not from non-living matter.
quiz.narration: According to Cell Theory, where do new cells come from?

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a light microscope from an electron microscope?
options: A light microscope can be used to view living cells; an electron microscope cannot
Both can view living cells equally well
An electron microscope uses light instead of electrons
A light microscope has higher resolution than an electron microscope
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — light microscopes can view living specimens; electron microscopes need a vacuum and cannot.
quiz.explainWrong: A light microscope, not an electron microscope, can be used to view living cells.
quiz.narration: Which statement correctly distinguishes a light microscope from an electron microscope?

quiz.question: Why do cells generally stay very small instead of growing very large?
options: A small size keeps the surface-area-to-volume ratio high enough for efficient exchange
Large cells cannot divide by mitosis
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a high surface-area-to-volume ratio keeps exchange of materials efficient.
quiz.explainWrong: The real reason is the surface-area-to-volume ratio: bigger cells struggle to exchange materials fast enough.
quiz.narration: Why do cells generally stay very small instead of growing very large?

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT considered part of the classical Cell Theory?
options: All viruses are made of cells
All organisms are composed of one or more cells
The cell is the basic unit of structure and function
Cells arise only from pre-existing cells
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — viruses are not made of cells, so this statement is NOT part of Cell Theory.
quiz.explainWrong: Viruses are not made of cells — that statement is the false one, and NOT part of Cell Theory.
quiz.narration: Which of the following is NOT considered part of the classical Cell Theory?

subtopics.title: Cell Structure: Organelles and Their Functions

stories.sub: A cell is a tiny, busy factory
stories.heading: Meet the departments
list: The nucleus is the head office — it holds the master instructions (DNA) and directs activity.
Mitochondria are the power plants — they release energy from food during respiration.
Ribosomes are the workshops — they assemble proteins from instructions sent by the nucleus.
The cell membrane is the factory gate — it controls exactly what goes in and out.
stories.narration: Think of a cell as a tiny factory. The nucleus is the head office holding the master instructions. Mitochondria are the power plants. Ribosomes are the workshops that assemble proteins. And the cell membrane is the factory gate controlling what goes in and out.

stories.sub: Mitochondria used to be free-living bacteria
stories.heading: The endosymbiotic theory
list: This theory proposes that mitochondria were once independent bacteria.
Billions of years ago, a larger cell engulfed one of these bacteria instead of digesting it.
The two began living together permanently — the bacterium became the mitochondrion we know today.
Evidence: mitochondria have their own small circle of DNA, separate from the nucleus, just like bacteria do.
stories.narration: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria were once independent bacteria. A larger cell engulfed one instead of digesting it, and the two began living together permanently. Mitochondria still carry their own small circle of DNA today, just like bacteria do.

lessons.heading: The nucleus
list: Bound by a nuclear envelope with pores that let materials pass through.
Contains chromatin (DNA + protein) which condenses into chromosomes during cell division.
Contains the nucleolus, which manufactures ribosomes.
Controls the cell's activities and carries the hereditary information passed to offspring.
lessons.sub: The nucleus is the cell's head office and its DNA archive in one.
lessons.narration: The nucleus is bound by a nuclear envelope, contains chromatin that condenses into chromosomes during division, and controls the cell's activities and hereditary information.

lessons.heading: Mitochondria
list: Site of aerobic respiration, where energy is released from glucose and stored as ATP.
Has a folded inner membrane (cristae) that increases surface area for respiration reactions.
Cells with high energy demand, like muscle cells, contain many mitochondria.
lessons.sub: More mitochondria usually means more energy demand.
lessons.narration: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy from glucose and storing it as ATP. Their folded inner membrane, called cristae, increases surface area for these reactions.

lessons.heading: Ribosomes
list: Tiny structures, either free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Site of protein synthesis — they read genetic instructions (mRNA) and link amino acids together.
Not membrane-bound, unlike most other organelles.
lessons.sub: Every protein in your body was assembled on a ribosome.
lessons.narration: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis, reading genetic instructions and linking amino acids together. Unlike most organelles, they are not membrane-bound.

lessons.heading: Endoplasmic reticulum
list: Rough ER: studded with ribosomes; folds and transports proteins made by those ribosomes.
Smooth ER: no ribosomes; makes lipids and helps detoxify certain substances.
Forms a network of membranes connecting different parts of the cell.
lessons.sub: Rough ER handles proteins, smooth ER handles lipids.
lessons.narration: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is studded with ribosomes and transports the proteins they make. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum has no ribosomes and instead makes lipids and helps detoxify substances.

lessons.heading: Golgi apparatus
list: A stack of flattened, membrane-bound sacs.
Receives proteins from the ER, modifies them (e.g. adds sugar groups), then packages them into vesicles.
Sends finished products to their correct destination inside or outside the cell.
lessons.sub: Think of it as the factory's dispatch department.
lessons.narration: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies and packages them into vesicles, and sends them to their correct destination.

lessons.heading: Lysosomes
list: Small sacs containing digestive enzymes.
Break down worn-out organelles, food particles, and foreign material such as bacteria inside the cell.
Sometimes called the cell's recycling centre.
lessons.sub: Lysosomes keep the cell's interior clean and recycled.
lessons.narration: Lysosomes are small sacs containing digestive enzymes. They break down worn-out organelles, food particles and foreign material, acting as the cell's recycling centre.

lessons.heading: Cell membrane — the fluid mosaic model
list: Made mainly of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins floating within it, like tiles in a mosaic.
It is selectively permeable — it allows some substances through freely and restricts others.
Controls movement of substances in and out of the cell via diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
lessons.sub: ‘Fluid mosaic’ describes both the flexible layer and the scattered proteins in it.
lessons.narration: The fluid mosaic model describes the cell membrane as a phospholipid bilayer with proteins floating within it. It is selectively permeable, controlling what moves in and out by diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

quiz.question: Which organelle contains chromatin and controls the cell's activities?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the nucleus contains chromatin and controls cell activities.
quiz.explainWrong: That's the nucleus — it contains chromatin and directs the cell's activities.
quiz.narration: Which organelle contains chromatin and controls the cell's activities?

quiz.question: Which organelle is the main site of aerobic respiration and ATP production?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — mitochondria are the main site of aerobic respiration and ATP production.
quiz.explainWrong: That's the mitochondrion — the site of aerobic respiration and ATP production.
quiz.narration: Which organelle is the main site of aerobic respiration and ATP production?

quiz.question: Which organelle modifies and packages proteins for transport out of the cell?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins into vesicles.
quiz.explainWrong: That's the Golgi apparatus — it modifies and packages proteins for transport.
quiz.narration: Which organelle modifies and packages proteins for transport out of the cell?

quiz.question: According to the fluid mosaic model, the cell membrane is mainly composed of…?
options: A phospholipid bilayer with floating proteins
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a phospholipid bilayer with proteins scattered through it, like tiles in a mosaic.
quiz.explainWrong: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with floating proteins — not cellulose or chromatin.
quiz.narration: According to the fluid mosaic model, the cell membrane is mainly composed of what?

stories.sub: Two factories, two blueprints
stories.heading: Why plant and animal cells look different
list: Plants can't run from danger — they must stand firm and grow toward light, so their cells build in rigid support.
Animals move around to find food and escape threats, so their cells stay flexible instead of rigid.
Every structural difference between the two cell types traces back to this one difference in lifestyle.
stories.narration: Plants can't run from danger, so their cells build in rigid support to stand firm and grow toward light. Animals move around instead, so their cells stay flexible. Every structural difference between the two traces back to this one difference in lifestyle.

stories.sub: Why a leaf feels firm but your skin feels soft
stories.heading: Turgor pressure at work
list: A plant cell's large vacuole fills with water and pushes outward against its rigid cell wall.
This water pressure, called turgor pressure, is what keeps leaves and stems crisp and upright.
Animal cells have no cell wall to push against, so tissue stays soft and flexible instead.
stories.narration: A plant cell's large vacuole fills with water and pushes outward against its rigid cell wall. This turgor pressure is what keeps leaves and stems crisp. Animal cells have no wall to push against, so their tissue stays soft.

lessons.heading: Cell wall
list: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall made of cellulose, outside the cell membrane.
It gives shape, support and protection.
Animal cells have no cell wall — only a flexible cell membrane.
lessons.sub: Cell wall = present in plants, absent in animals.
lessons.narration: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall made of cellulose, giving shape, support and protection. Animal cells have no cell wall — only a flexible cell membrane.

lessons.heading: Chloroplasts
list: Plant cells, in their green parts, contain chloroplasts with chlorophyll for photosynthesis.
Chloroplasts trap light energy and use it to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
Animal cells have no chloroplasts and cannot photosynthesise.
lessons.sub: Chloroplast = present in (green) plant cells, absent in animal cells.
lessons.narration: Plant cells contain chloroplasts with chlorophyll, which trap light energy for photosynthesis. Animal cells have no chloroplasts and cannot photosynthesise.

lessons.heading: Vacuole size
list: Mature plant cells usually have one large, permanent central vacuole for storage and maintaining turgor pressure.
Animal cells may have several small, temporary vacuoles instead.
lessons.sub: One big permanent vacuole (plant) vs several small temporary ones (animal).
lessons.narration: Mature plant cells usually have one large permanent vacuole for storage and turgor pressure. Animal cells may have several small, temporary vacuoles instead.

lessons.heading: Shape
list: Plant cells tend to have a fixed, regular shape, often rectangular, due to the cell wall.
Animal cells tend to have irregular, rounded shapes since they only have a flexible membrane.
lessons.sub: Fixed shape (plant) vs irregular shape (animal).
lessons.narration: Plant cells tend to have a fixed, regular shape because of the cell wall. Animal cells tend to have irregular, rounded shapes since they only have a flexible membrane.

lessons.heading: Centrioles
list: Animal cells contain centrioles that help organise spindle fibres during cell division.
Most plant cells lack centrioles.
lessons.sub: Centrioles = present in animal cells, generally absent in plant cells.
lessons.narration: Animal cells contain centrioles that help organise spindle fibres during cell division. Most plant cells lack centrioles.

lessons.heading: Summary: the 4 key differences
list: Cell wall — present in plants, absent in animals.
Chloroplast — present in green plant cells, absent in animals.
Vacuole — one large permanent one in plants, small/temporary in animals.
Centriole — present in animals, generally absent in plants.
lessons.sub: WAEC often gives a labelled diagram and asks you to identify whether it's a plant or animal cell from just one of these features.
lessons.narration: The four key differences to remember: cell wall, chloroplast, vacuole size, and centrioles. WAEC often gives a labelled diagram and asks you to identify plant or animal cell from just one of these.

quiz.question: What structure gives plant cells a rigid, fixed shape that animal cells lack?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the cellulose cell wall gives plant cells their rigid, fixed shape.
quiz.explainWrong: It's the cellulose cell wall — animal cells lack this and only have a flexible membrane.
quiz.narration: What structure gives plant cells a rigid, fixed shape that animal cells lack?

quiz.question: Chloroplasts, which carry out photosynthesis, are found in…
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — chloroplasts are found only in plant cells (their green parts).
quiz.explainWrong: Chloroplasts are found only in plant cells, not animal cells.
quiz.narration: Chloroplasts, which carry out photosynthesis, are found in which cells?

quiz.question: A mature plant cell typically has one large permanent vacuole. What is one of its main roles?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the large vacuole maintains turgor pressure, keeping the plant firm.
quiz.explainWrong: The large vacuole's main role is maintaining turgor pressure and support.
quiz.narration: A mature plant cell's large permanent vacuole has what main role?

quiz.question: Which structure, involved in organising spindle fibres during division, is found in animal cells but is generally absent in plant cells?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — centrioles organise spindle fibres in animal cells and are generally absent in plant cells.
quiz.explainWrong: That's the centriole — found in animal cells, generally absent in plant cells.
quiz.narration: Which structure, involved in organising spindle fibres during division, is found in animal cells but generally absent in plant cells?

stories.sub: The man who saw ‘animalcules’
stories.heading: Leeuwenhoek's tiny discovery
list: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built simple but powerful microscopes by hand.
In the 1670s, he became the first person to observe bacteria, calling the tiny moving organisms he saw ‘animalcules’.
He had no idea he was looking at some of the simplest cells on Earth — prokaryotic cells.
stories.narration: In the 1670s, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built simple but powerful microscopes and became the first person to observe bacteria, calling them animalcules. He had no idea he was looking at prokaryotic cells — some of the simplest cells on Earth.

stories.sub: Earth's first citizens
stories.heading: Life before the nucleus
list: Prokaryote-like organisms are thought to be among the earliest forms of life, roughly 3.5 billion years ago.
This was long before any nucleus-containing (eukaryotic) cell existed.
Every eukaryotic cell alive today — including yours — evolved from ancestors that started out this simple.
stories.narration: Prokaryote-like organisms are thought to be among the earliest forms of life, roughly three and a half billion years ago — long before any nucleus-containing cell existed.

lessons.heading: Defining the two types
list: Prokaryotic cells have no true, membrane-bound nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane.
lessons.sub: ‘Pro-karyote’ = before a nucleus. ‘Eu-karyote’ = true nucleus.
lessons.narration: Prokaryotic cells have no true, membrane-bound nucleus. Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane.

lessons.heading: Nucleoid vs nucleus
list: In prokaryotes, DNA lies free in the cytoplasm, in a region called the nucleoid.
In eukaryotes, DNA is enclosed within a membrane-bound nucleus.
lessons.sub: No membrane around the DNA = prokaryote. Membrane around the DNA = eukaryote.
lessons.narration: In prokaryotes, DNA lies free in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid. In eukaryotes, DNA is enclosed within a membrane-bound nucleus.

lessons.heading: Size comparison
list: Prokaryotic cells are generally much smaller: about 0.1–5 micrometres.
Eukaryotic cells are generally larger: about 10–100 micrometres.
lessons.sub: Eukaryotic cells are typically 10 to 100 times bigger than prokaryotic cells.
lessons.narration: Prokaryotic cells are generally much smaller, about zero point one to five micrometres. Eukaryotic cells are generally larger, about ten to one hundred micrometres.

lessons.heading: Which organisms are which?
list: Prokaryotes: bacteria and archaea, e.g. Escherichia coli.
Eukaryotes: protists, fungi, plants and animals, e.g. Amoeba, yeast, humans.
lessons.sub: If it has a nucleus, it's a eukaryote — whatever kingdom it belongs to.
lessons.narration: Prokaryotes include bacteria and archaea, such as Escherichia coli. Eukaryotes include protists, fungi, plants and animals, such as Amoeba, yeast and humans.

lessons.heading: Organelles present
list: Eukaryotic cells contain membrane-bound organelles: mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, and more.
Prokaryotic cells lack these membrane-bound organelles.
lessons.sub: Eukaryotes are internally compartmentalised; prokaryotes mostly are not.
lessons.narration: Eukaryotic cells contain membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus. Prokaryotic cells lack these membrane-bound organelles.

lessons.heading: Reproduction
list: Prokaryotes reproduce mainly by binary fission — a simple splitting into two.
Eukaryotic cells reproduce by mitosis (body cells) or meiosis (sex cells), both more complex processes.
lessons.sub: Binary fission is simpler and faster than mitosis or meiosis.
lessons.narration: Prokaryotes reproduce mainly by binary fission, a simple splitting into two. Eukaryotic cells reproduce by mitosis or meiosis, both more complex processes.

quiz.question: The main feature that distinguishes a eukaryotic cell from a prokaryotic cell is…
options: The presence of a cell membrane
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a true, membrane-bound nucleus is the defining feature of eukaryotic cells.
quiz.explainWrong: The defining feature is a true, membrane-bound nucleus — both cell types have a membrane and cytoplasm.
quiz.narration: The main feature that distinguishes a eukaryotic cell from a prokaryotic cell is what?

quiz.question: In a prokaryotic cell, where is the genetic material (DNA) mainly located?
options: Free in the cytoplasm, in a region called the nucleoid
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — prokaryotic DNA lies free in the cytoplasm, in the nucleoid region.
quiz.explainWrong: Prokaryotic DNA lies free in the cytoplasm, in a region called the nucleoid — not inside a membrane-bound nucleus.
quiz.narration: In a prokaryotic cell, where is the genetic material mainly located?

quiz.question: Which of the following is an example of a prokaryotic organism?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Escherichia coli is a bacterium, a prokaryotic organism.
quiz.explainWrong: Escherichia coli is the prokaryote here — the others are all eukaryotic.
quiz.narration: Which of the following is an example of a prokaryotic organism?

quiz.question: Which of these organelles would you expect to find in a eukaryotic cell but NOT in a typical prokaryotic cell?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotes, not typical prokaryotes.
quiz.explainWrong: It's the mitochondrion — note that ribosomes are actually present in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
quiz.narration: Which of these organelles would you expect to find in a eukaryotic cell but not in a typical prokaryotic cell?

stories.sub: From a single brick to a whole city
stories.heading: Cell → tissue → organ → system → organism
list: A single cell is like one brick.
Similar cells grouped together form a tissue — like a wall made of bricks.
Different tissues combine to form an organ — like a whole room built from several walls.
Organs combine into organ systems, and organ systems combine into a whole organism — the whole city.
stories.narration: Imagine zooming a camera out from a single brick to a whole city. A single cell is like one brick. Similar cells grouped together form a tissue, like a wall. Different tissues combine into an organ, like a room. And organs combine into systems, and systems into a whole organism — the whole city.

stories.sub: Departments in a company
stories.heading: Division of labour
list: A company has departments — sales, production, logistics — each specialising in one job.
A multicellular body has organ systems — digestive, circulatory, nervous — each specialising for survival.
In both cases, specialisation lets the whole system do far more than any single part could do alone.
stories.narration: Just as a company has departments like sales, production and logistics each specialising in one job, a multicellular body has organ systems like digestive, circulatory and nervous, each specialising for survival.

lessons.heading: The five levels
list: Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism.
Each level is built from the level directly below it.
lessons.sub: Learn this order exactly — WAEC frequently tests it directly.
lessons.narration: The levels of biological organisation, from smallest to largest, are: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, and organism. Each level is built from the level directly below it.

lessons.heading: What is a tissue?
list: A group of similar cells performing the same function.
Examples: epithelial tissue (covering/lining), muscle tissue (movement), nervous tissue (signalling), connective tissue (support).
lessons.sub: Similar cells + same function = tissue.
lessons.narration: A tissue is a group of similar cells performing the same function — examples include epithelial tissue, muscle tissue, nervous tissue and connective tissue.

lessons.heading: What is an organ?
list: A structure made of two or more different tissues working together to perform a specific function.
Example: the heart is made of muscle, connective and nervous tissue working together to pump blood.
lessons.sub: Different tissues + one shared function = organ.
lessons.narration: An organ is made of two or more different tissues working together for a specific function. For example, the heart combines muscle, connective and nervous tissue to pump blood.

lessons.heading: What is an organ system?
list: A group of organs working together for a broader function.
Example: the digestive system — mouth, stomach, intestines — breaks down and absorbs food.
lessons.sub: Different organs + one broader function = organ system.
lessons.narration: An organ system is a group of organs working together for a broader function. For example, the digestive system's mouth, stomach and intestines work together to break down and absorb food.

lessons.heading: Common human organ systems
list: Circulatory (transport), respiratory (gas exchange), digestive (nutrition).
Nervous (control), excretory (waste removal), reproductive (continuity of species).
lessons.sub: Each system has one clear headline job — learn the pairing.
lessons.narration: Common human organ systems include circulatory for transport, respiratory for gas exchange, digestive for nutrition, nervous for control, excretory for waste removal, and reproductive for continuity of the species.

lessons.heading: Don't mix up the levels
list: WAEC often gives a structure and asks you to identify its level: cell, tissue, organ or system.
Remember: an organ = combination of different tissues. A system = combination of organs.
lessons.sub: If it names one function made of several organs, it's a system, not an organ.
lessons.narration: WAEC often gives a structure and asks you to identify its level. Remember: an organ is a combination of different tissues, and a system is a combination of organs.

quiz.question: Arrange in increasing order of organisation: organ, cell, tissue, organ system.
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the order is cell, tissue, organ, then organ system.
quiz.explainWrong: The correct increasing order is cell, then tissue, then organ, then organ system.
quiz.narration: Arrange in increasing order of organisation: organ, cell, tissue, organ system.

quiz.question: A tissue is best defined as…
options: A group of similar cells performing the same function
Two or more organs working together
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a tissue is a group of similar cells performing the same function.
quiz.explainWrong: A tissue is a group of similar cells performing the same function, not a single cell or a group of organs.
quiz.narration: A tissue is best defined as what?

quiz.question: The heart is considered an organ because it is made up of…
options: Two or more different tissues working together for one function
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the heart combines muscle, connective and nervous tissue to work as one organ.
quiz.explainWrong: The heart is an organ because it combines two or more different tissues working together for one function.
quiz.narration: The heart is considered an organ because it is made up of what?

quiz.question: Which of these best describes an organ system?
options: A group of organs working together for a broader function, e.g. digestion
A tissue made of one cell type
The cell membrane of an organism
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — an organ system is a group of organs working together for a broader function.
quiz.explainWrong: An organ system is a group of organs working together for a broader function, such as digestion.
quiz.narration: Which of these best describes an organ system?

topics.title: Cell Division
topics.description: How cells reproduce themselves — the cell cycle, mitosis for growth and repair, and meiosis for making gametes.

stories.sub: The thread that carries instructions
stories.heading: How chromosomes got their name
list: Walther Flemming (1882) studied dividing cells and stained thread-like structures inside the nucleus with dye.
The threads absorbed the dye strongly, so he named them ‘chromosomes’ — Greek for ‘coloured body’.
He watched them split evenly between two new cells and correctly guessed they carried hereditary information.
Decades later, DNA was confirmed as the molecule chromosomes are actually made of.
stories.narration: In 1882, Walther Flemming studied dividing cells and stained thread-like structures inside the nucleus with dye. The threads absorbed colour so strongly he named them chromosomes, Greek for coloured body. He watched them split evenly between two new cells and correctly guessed they carried hereditary information.

stories.sub: Every second, millions of your cells divide
stories.heading: Growth, repair and replacement never stop
list: An adult human replaces billions of cells every day — skin, blood and gut-lining cells wear out constantly.
Without cell division, a cut would never heal and you would never have grown past a single fertilised egg.
Uncontrolled, badly-timed cell division is what causes cancer.
stories.narration: An adult human replaces billions of cells every day. Without cell division, a cut would never heal, and you would never have grown past a single fertilised egg. Uncontrolled, badly timed cell division is what causes cancer.

lessons.heading: What is the cell cycle?
list: The cell cycle is the repeating sequence a cell goes through: growth, DNA copying, and division into two cells.
It has two main stages: interphase (growth and DNA replication) and the mitotic phase (division).
Interphase takes up about 90% of the cycle's time — division itself is relatively quick.
lessons.sub: A cell spends most of its ‘life’ preparing, not dividing.
lessons.narration: The cell cycle is the repeating sequence a cell goes through: growth, DNA copying, and division into two cells. It has two main stages — interphase, which is growth and DNA replication, and the mitotic phase, which is division. Interphase takes up about ninety percent of the cycle's time.

lessons.heading: What happens before a cell divides
list: G1 phase: the cell grows and carries out its normal functions.
S phase: the cell copies its entire DNA, so each chromosome now has two identical halves.
G2 phase: the cell grows further and builds the machinery it needs to divide.
lessons.sub: G1, S, G2 — growth, copy, get-ready.
lessons.narration: In G1 phase, the cell grows and carries out its normal functions. In S phase, the cell copies its entire DNA, so each chromosome now has two identical halves. In G2 phase, the cell grows further and builds the machinery it needs to divide.

lessons.heading: Chromosomes, chromatids and genes
list: A chromosome is a single tightly-coiled thread of DNA.
After DNA replication, each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere.
A gene is a short section of DNA that codes for one characteristic; a single chromosome carries many genes.
lessons.sub: Chromatid = one half of a copied chromosome, not a separate chromosome.
lessons.narration: A chromosome is a single tightly coiled thread of DNA. After DNA replication, each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere. A gene is a short section of DNA that codes for one characteristic, and a single chromosome carries many genes.

lessons.heading: Diploid body cells, haploid sex cells
list: Human body (somatic) cells are diploid: they contain 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs.
One chromosome of each pair comes from the mother, one from the father.
Human sex cells (gametes) are haploid: they contain only 23 chromosomes, one from each pair.
lessons.sub: WAEC often gives an organism's diploid number and asks for the number in its gametes — just halve it.
lessons.narration: Human body cells are diploid: they contain forty-six chromosomes, in twenty-three pairs, one of each pair from the mother and one from the father. Human sex cells, or gametes, are haploid: they contain only twenty-three chromosomes, one from each pair.

lessons.heading: Two ways a cell can divide
list: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells — used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells — used only to make gametes for sexual reproduction.
The next two sub-topics look at each process card by card.
lessons.sub: Same-copy division vs variety-making division.
lessons.narration: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells, used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells, used only to make gametes for sexual reproduction.

quiz.question: A normal human body cell contains how many chromosomes?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — human body cells are diploid, with 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.
quiz.explainWrong: Human body cells are diploid and contain 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs — not 23, 92 or 44.
quiz.narration: A normal human body cell contains how many chromosomes?

quiz.question: After DNA replication, what does a chromosome consist of?
options: Two sister chromatids joined at a centromere
A single unchanged strand of DNA
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — replication produces two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere, not two separate chromosomes.
quiz.explainWrong: After replication a chromosome has two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere — they aren't separate chromosomes yet.
quiz.narration: After DNA replication, what does a chromosome consist of?

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a diploid and a haploid cell?
options: A diploid cell has two full sets of chromosomes; a haploid cell has one
A diploid cell has no nucleus; a haploid cell does
A haploid cell is always larger
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — diploid (2n) means two full chromosome sets, as in body cells; haploid (n) means one set, as in gametes.
quiz.explainWrong: The difference is chromosome number: diploid cells carry two full sets, haploid cells (gametes) carry only one.
quiz.narration: What is the key difference between a diploid and a haploid cell?

quiz.question: Which type of cell division is used for growth and repair of body tissue?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — mitosis produces genetically identical diploid cells, exactly what growth and repair need.
quiz.explainWrong: Growth and repair use mitosis, which produces identical diploid cells — meiosis is only for making gametes.
quiz.narration: Which type of cell division is used for growth and repair of body tissue?

stories.sub: A dance with four steady steps
stories.heading: Mitosis is choreography, not chaos
list: Under a microscope, mitosis looks dramatic — but it always follows the same four-stage order.
Biologists use the acronym PMAT (Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase) to remember the sequence.
Every stage exists to make sure each new cell gets one complete, undamaged copy of every chromosome.
stories.narration: Under a microscope, mitosis looks dramatic, but it always follows the same four-stage order. Biologists use the acronym PMAT — Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase — to remember the sequence. Every stage exists to make sure each new cell gets one complete, undamaged copy of every chromosome.

stories.sub: When the count goes wrong
stories.heading: Why an exact copy matters
list: If chromosomes are shared out unevenly during mitosis, the resulting cells can have too many or too few.
In humans, this kind of error is linked to some cancers and developmental conditions.
That is why mitosis has built-in checkpoints that pause the cycle if something looks wrong.
stories.narration: If chromosomes are shared out unevenly during mitosis, the resulting cells can have too many or too few. In humans this kind of error is linked to some cancers and developmental conditions, which is why mitosis has built-in checkpoints that pause the cycle if something looks wrong.

lessons.heading: Prophase — getting ready
list: Chromosomes condense from loose threads into short, thick, visible structures.
The nuclear membrane breaks down.
Spindle fibres begin growing from opposite ends (poles) of the cell.
lessons.sub: P for Prophase, P for Packing up.
lessons.narration: In prophase, chromosomes condense from loose threads into short, thick, visible structures. The nuclear membrane breaks down, and spindle fibres begin growing from opposite ends of the cell.

lessons.heading: Metaphase — lining up
list: Chromosomes, still as sister-chromatid pairs, line up along the middle (equator) of the cell.
Spindle fibres from each pole attach to the centromere of every chromosome.
This precise alignment is what allows an exactly equal split in the next stage.
lessons.sub: M for Metaphase, M for the Middle.
lessons.narration: In metaphase, chromosomes line up along the middle of the cell, still as sister chromatid pairs. Spindle fibres from each pole attach to the centromere of every chromosome, allowing an exactly equal split in the next stage.

lessons.heading: Anaphase — pulling apart
list: The centromere of each chromosome splits, separating the two sister chromatids.
Spindle fibres shorten, pulling one chromatid to each pole of the cell.
Each chromatid is now counted as its own full chromosome.
lessons.sub: A for Anaphase, A for Apart.
lessons.narration: In anaphase, the centromere of each chromosome splits, separating the two sister chromatids. Spindle fibres shorten, pulling one chromatid to each pole of the cell — each chromatid now counts as its own full chromosome.

lessons.heading: Telophase and cytokinesis — two new cells
list: A nuclear membrane reforms around each full set of chromosomes at the two poles.
Chromosomes uncoil back into loose threads.
Cytokinesis then splits the cytoplasm, producing two separate, genetically identical daughter cells.
lessons.sub: T for Telophase, T for Two nuclei.
lessons.narration: In telophase, a nuclear membrane reforms around each full set of chromosomes at the two poles, and the chromosomes uncoil. Cytokinesis then splits the cytoplasm, producing two separate, genetically identical daughter cells.

lessons.heading: What makes mitosis's products special
list: Mitosis produces exactly 2 daughter cells per division, not 4.
Both daughter cells are diploid — the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
Both daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent and to each other (barring rare mutation).
lessons.sub: 2 cells, same number, identical genes — the mitosis signature WAEC tests.
lessons.narration: Mitosis produces exactly two daughter cells per division, not four. Both are diploid, with the same chromosome number as the parent cell, and both are genetically identical to the parent and to each other.

quiz.question: Put the stages of mitosis in the correct order.
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — remember PMAT: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase.
quiz.explainWrong: The correct order is Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase — remembered as PMAT.
quiz.narration: Put the stages of mitosis in the correct order.

quiz.question: During which stage do sister chromatids separate and get pulled to opposite poles?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — in anaphase, the centromere splits and spindle fibres pull the chromatids apart.
quiz.explainWrong: Chromatid separation happens in anaphase, after they have lined up in metaphase.
quiz.narration: During which stage do sister chromatids separate and get pulled to opposite poles?

quiz.question: Chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell during which stage?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — metaphase is the lining-up stage, letting spindle fibres attach precisely to every centromere.
quiz.explainWrong: Lining up at the cell's equator is metaphase, not anaphase, telophase or prophase.
quiz.narration: Chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell during which stage?

quiz.question: How many daughter cells does one mitotic division produce, and what is their chromosome number compared to the parent?
options: Two daughter cells, same (diploid) chromosome number as the parent
Four daughter cells, half the chromosome number
Two daughter cells, half the chromosome number
One daughter cell, double the chromosome number
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — mitosis makes 2 diploid daughter cells, genetically identical to the parent.
quiz.explainWrong: Mitosis produces 2 daughter cells with the same diploid chromosome number as the parent, not 4 or half.
quiz.narration: How many daughter cells does one mitotic division produce, and what is their chromosome number compared to the parent?

stories.sub: One division wasn't enough
stories.heading: Why sex cells need a special kind of division
list: If gametes were made by ordinary mitosis, they would be diploid — and fertilisation would double the chromosome number every generation.
Meiosis solves this by halving the chromosome number, so fertilisation restores the normal diploid count.
It does this with two divisions back to back, not one.
stories.narration: If gametes were made by ordinary mitosis, they would be diploid, and fertilisation would double the chromosome number every generation. Meiosis solves this by halving the chromosome number, using two divisions back to back instead of one, so fertilisation restores the normal diploid count.

stories.sub: Why siblings aren't identical
stories.heading: Meiosis is where genetic variety is born
list: During meiosis, chromosome pairs swap sections in a process called crossing over.
Chromosome pairs also separate into gametes independently of each other (independent assortment).
This is the main reason full siblings share genes but still look and differ from one another.
stories.narration: During meiosis, chromosome pairs swap sections in a process called crossing over, and pairs separate into gametes independently of each other. This is the main reason full siblings share genes but still look different from one another.

lessons.heading: What meiosis is for
list: Meiosis is the type of division that produces gametes: sperm and egg cells in animals, pollen and ovules in plants.
It takes one diploid cell and produces four haploid cells.
Only reproductive organs (testes, ovaries; anthers, ovaries in flowers) carry out meiosis.
lessons.sub: Meiosis = the gamete-making division.
lessons.narration: Meiosis is the type of division that produces gametes — sperm and egg cells in animals, pollen and ovules in plants. It takes one diploid cell and produces four haploid cells, and only reproductive organs carry it out.

lessons.heading: Meiosis I and Meiosis II
list: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosome pairs, halving the chromosome number (diploid → haploid).
Meiosis II then separates sister chromatids, similar to a mitotic division — but starting from haploid cells.
The result of both rounds together: four haploid cells from one starting diploid cell.
lessons.sub: DNA is copied only once, but the cell divides twice.
lessons.narration: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosome pairs, halving the chromosome number from diploid to haploid. Meiosis II then separates sister chromatids, similar to a mitotic division, but starting from haploid cells. The result: four haploid cells from one starting diploid cell.

lessons.heading: Crossing over
list: Early in Meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair up tightly, a process called synapsis.
Paired chromosomes can swap equivalent sections of DNA at points called chiasmata — this is crossing over.
Crossing over creates new combinations of genes that didn't exist on either original chromosome.
lessons.sub: Crossing over shuffles genes between the chromosome you got from mum and the one from dad.
lessons.narration: Early in meiosis one, homologous chromosomes pair up tightly and can swap equivalent sections of DNA at points called chiasmata — this is crossing over. It creates new combinations of genes that didn't exist on either original chromosome.

lessons.heading: Independent assortment
list: When homologous pairs line up in Meiosis I, which pole each chromosome faces is random.
With 23 chromosome pairs in humans, this randomness alone gives over 8 million possible chromosome combinations per gamete.
Combined with crossing over, this is why (apart from identical twins) no two gametes are ever genetically the same.
lessons.sub: Random orientation × random crossing over = enormous genetic variety.
lessons.narration: When homologous pairs line up in meiosis one, which pole each chromosome faces is random. With twenty-three chromosome pairs in humans, this alone gives over eight million possible combinations per gamete — which is why no two gametes are ever genetically the same.

lessons.heading: Mitosis vs meiosis — the comparison WAEC loves
list: Divisions: mitosis divides once; meiosis divides twice.
Daughter cells: mitosis makes 2 diploid, identical cells; meiosis makes 4 haploid, genetically different cells.
Purpose: mitosis is for growth, repair and asexual reproduction; meiosis is only for making gametes.
lessons.sub: If a question mentions ‘gametes’ or ‘halved chromosome number’, the answer is meiosis.
lessons.narration: Mitosis divides once and makes two diploid, identical daughter cells, for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis divides twice and makes four haploid, genetically different daughter cells, only to make gametes.

quiz.question: Why must gametes be haploid rather than diploid?
options: So that fertilisation restores the normal diploid chromosome number
So that gametes can move faster
So that gametes never carry mutations
So that only one parent contributes chromosomes
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — halving the number in gametes means fertilisation (fusing two gametes) restores the normal diploid count.
quiz.explainWrong: Gametes are haploid so that when two of them fuse at fertilisation, the diploid number is restored, not doubled.
quiz.narration: Why must gametes be haploid rather than diploid?

quiz.question: One diploid cell undergoing meiosis produces how many cells, and of what chromosome number?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — meiosis's two divisions turn one diploid cell into four haploid cells.
quiz.explainWrong: Meiosis produces four haploid cells from one diploid cell, not two diploid cells like mitosis.
quiz.narration: One diploid cell undergoing meiosis produces how many cells, and of what chromosome number?

quiz.question: What is crossing over?
options: The swapping of DNA sections between paired homologous chromosomes
The movement of a whole chromosome to one pole
The joining of two unrelated gametes
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — crossing over is the exchange of equivalent DNA sections between homologous chromosomes, creating new gene combinations.
quiz.explainWrong: Crossing over is the swapping of DNA sections between paired homologous chromosomes — not centromere splitting or gamete fusion.
quiz.narration: What is crossing over?

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes mitosis from meiosis?
options: Mitosis makes 2 identical diploid cells; meiosis makes 4 different haploid cells
Mitosis makes 4 identical cells; meiosis makes 2 different cells
Both processes make exactly the same kind of cell
Meiosis is used for tissue repair, mitosis for making gametes
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — mitosis: 2 identical diploid cells. Meiosis: 4 genetically different haploid cells.
quiz.explainWrong: Mitosis produces 2 identical diploid cells; meiosis produces 4 genetically different haploid cells — the roles aren't reversed.
quiz.narration: Which statement correctly distinguishes mitosis from meiosis?

topics.title: Classification of Living Things
topics.description: Why and how biologists sort every living thing into a nested system of groups, from kingdom down to species.

stories.sub: One creature, a hundred different names
stories.heading: Why biology needed a filing system
list: Before formal classification, the same plant or animal could have a different local name in every region and language.
Scientists writing to each other across countries often had no idea they were describing the same organism.
Classification (taxonomy) was invented to give every organism one agreed place in a shared system.
stories.narration: Before formal classification, the same plant or animal could have a different local name in every region and language. Scientists writing to each other across countries often had no idea they were describing the same organism. Classification, or taxonomy, was invented to give every organism one agreed place in a shared system.

stories.sub: One Swedish botanist, one nested system
stories.heading: Carl Linnaeus and the hierarchy we still use
list: Carl Linnaeus (1735) organised living things into a nested hierarchy of groups within groups.
Each level groups organisms that share more and more features the further down you go.
Modern classification has added DNA evidence, but Linnaeus's nested structure is still the backbone.
stories.narration: Carl Linnaeus, in 1735, organised living things into a nested hierarchy of groups within groups, where each level groups organisms that share more and more features the further down you go. Modern classification has added DNA evidence, but his nested structure is still the backbone.

lessons.heading: What is classification?
list: Classification is the sorting of living things into groups based on shared characteristics.
It makes the huge diversity of life easier to study, compare and communicate about.
The scientific study of classification is called taxonomy.
lessons.sub: Classification turns millions of species into a searchable system.
lessons.narration: Classification is the sorting of living things into groups based on shared characteristics. It makes the huge diversity of life easier to study, compare and communicate about. The scientific study of classification is called taxonomy.

lessons.heading: The seven main taxonomic ranks
list: From broadest to narrowest: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
Each rank contains one or more groups of the rank below it — a Kingdom contains many Phyla, a Phylum contains many Classes, and so on.
A common memory aid: ‘King Philip Came Over For Good Soup’.
lessons.sub: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species — in that order, every time.
lessons.narration: From broadest to narrowest, the seven main ranks are Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species. Each rank contains one or more groups of the rank below it. A common memory aid is King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

lessons.heading: As you go down the hierarchy
list: The number of organisms in each group gets smaller.
The number of shared features between members of the group gets larger.
Species is the smallest, most specific rank — members of a species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
lessons.sub: Fewer members, more in common — that's the trend going down the ranks.
lessons.narration: As you move down the hierarchy, the number of organisms in each group gets smaller, while the number of features they share gets larger. Species is the smallest, most specific rank — members of a species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

lessons.heading: Classifying the human species
list: Kingdom: Animalia. Phylum: Chordata (has a backbone). Class: Mammalia (has hair, produces milk).
Order: Primates. Family: Hominidae. Genus: Homo. Species: sapiens.
Full scientific name: Homo sapiens — genus first, species second.
lessons.sub: Humans share Class Mammalia with dogs and whales, but only Species with other humans.
lessons.narration: Humans are classified as Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Primates, Family Hominidae, Genus Homo, and Species sapiens — giving the full scientific name Homo sapiens.

lessons.heading: Common WAEC pitfalls on the hierarchy
list: Do not reverse the order — Kingdom is always the broadest, Species always the narrowest.
A ‘Class’ in biology has nothing to do with a classroom — don't confuse it with everyday English.
WAEC often gives a partial hierarchy and asks you to fill in the missing rank — know the sequence by heart.
lessons.sub: If you can recite King Philip Came Over For Good Soup instantly, this question type is free marks.
lessons.narration: Do not reverse the order — Kingdom is always the broadest, Species always the narrowest. WAEC often gives a partial hierarchy and asks you to fill in the missing rank, so know the sequence by heart.

quiz.question: Which is the correct order of taxonomic ranks, from broadest to narrowest?
options: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Family, Order, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Family, Order, Species, Genus
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species, from broadest to narrowest.
quiz.explainWrong: The correct order, broadest to narrowest, is Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
quiz.narration: Which is the correct order of taxonomic ranks, from broadest to narrowest?

quiz.question: As you move down the taxonomic hierarchy from Kingdom to Species, what happens?
options: The number of organisms in each group decreases and shared features increase
The number of organisms increases and shared features decrease
Both the number of organisms and shared features increase
Nothing changes except the group's name
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — lower ranks contain fewer organisms that share more features in common.
quiz.explainWrong: Moving down the hierarchy, groups get smaller in number but members share more features — not the reverse.
quiz.narration: As you move down the taxonomic hierarchy from Kingdom to Species, what happens?

quiz.question: In the classification of humans, Homo sapiens, what does ‘Homo’ represent?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — in a scientific name, the first word is always the genus; the second is the species.
quiz.explainWrong: ‘Homo’ is the genus; ‘sapiens’ is the species — the genus always comes first in a scientific name.
quiz.narration: In the classification of humans, Homo sapiens, what does ‘Homo’ represent?

quiz.question: Two organisms belonging to the same species are expected to be able to
options: live in exactly the same habitat only
have completely identical genes with no variation
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the ability to interbreed and produce fertile offspring is the standard definition of a species.
quiz.explainWrong: Members of a species can interbreed and produce fertile offspring — habitat and identical genes are not the definition.
quiz.narration: Two organisms belonging to the same species are expected to be able to

stories.sub: From two boxes to five
stories.heading: Why ‘plant’ or ‘animal’ wasn't enough
list: For centuries, living things were sorted into only two kingdoms: Plants and Animals.
But bacteria, fungi and single-celled organisms didn't fit either box neatly.
In 1969, Robert Whittaker proposed five kingdoms, based on cell structure and how organisms feed.
stories.narration: For centuries, living things were sorted into only two kingdoms: plants and animals. But bacteria, fungi and single-celled organisms didn't fit either box neatly. In 1969, Robert Whittaker proposed five kingdoms instead, based on cell structure and how organisms feed.

stories.sub: A kingdom you meet every day
stories.heading: Fungi aren't plants
list: Mushrooms were long grouped with plants because both are rooted in place and don't move.
But fungi don't photosynthesise — they absorb nutrients from their surroundings, more like a very slow, spread-out form of feeding.
This feeding difference is exactly why fungi got their own kingdom.
stories.narration: Mushrooms were long grouped with plants because both stay rooted in place. But fungi don't photosynthesise — they absorb nutrients from their surroundings instead — which is exactly why fungi got their own kingdom.

lessons.heading: The five kingdoms at a glance
list: Kingdom Monera — bacteria; no true nucleus.
Kingdom Protista — mostly single-celled, has a nucleus (e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium).
Kingdom Fungi, Kingdom Plantae, Kingdom Animalia — the three multicellular kingdoms.
lessons.sub: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
lessons.narration: The five kingdoms are Monera, which are bacteria with no true nucleus; Protista, mostly single-celled organisms with a nucleus; and then Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, the three multicellular kingdoms.

lessons.heading: Bacteria — life without a nucleus
list: Monerans are prokaryotes: single-celled organisms whose DNA floats freely, not enclosed in a nucleus.
They are the smallest and most numerous living things on Earth.
Examples: E. coli, Rhizobium (nitrogen-fixing soil bacteria).
lessons.sub: No nucleus is the single feature that defines this kingdom.
lessons.narration: Monerans are prokaryotes — single-celled organisms whose DNA floats freely, not enclosed in a nucleus. They are the smallest and most numerous living things on Earth, including bacteria like E. coli.

lessons.heading: Protists — the ‘odds and ends’ kingdom
list: Protists are eukaryotes (have a true nucleus), mostly single-celled.
Some resemble tiny animals (Amoeba, Paramecium), some resemble tiny plants (algae like Spirogyra).
They are grouped together mainly because they don't fit neatly into Fungi, Plantae or Animalia.
lessons.sub: If it's single-celled but has a nucleus, it's probably a Protist.
lessons.narration: Protists are eukaryotes, mostly single-celled, that don't fit neatly into fungi, plants or animals. Some, like Amoeba, resemble tiny animals; others, like Spirogyra, resemble tiny plants.

lessons.heading: Fungi — feeders by absorption
list: Fungi have cell walls made of chitin, not cellulose like plants.
They cannot photosynthesise; they feed by releasing digestive enzymes onto food and absorbing the products.
Examples: mushrooms, yeast, bread mould (Rhizopus).
lessons.sub: Chitin cell wall + absorptive feeding = Fungi, not Plantae.
lessons.narration: Fungi have cell walls made of chitin, not cellulose. They cannot photosynthesise — instead they release digestive enzymes onto their food and absorb the products, as in mushrooms, yeast and bread mould.

lessons.heading: Plantae vs Animalia — the quick test
list: Plantae: cells have a cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts; make their own food by photosynthesis.
Animalia: cells have no cell wall and no chloroplasts; feed on other organisms (heterotrophic).
If a question mentions chloroplasts or a cellulose wall, the answer is a plant cell or Kingdom Plantae.
lessons.sub: Cell wall + chloroplasts = plant. No cell wall, no chloroplasts = animal.
lessons.narration: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts and make their own food by photosynthesis. Animal cells have no cell wall and no chloroplasts, and feed on other organisms.

quiz.question: Which kingdom consists of organisms whose cells have no true nucleus?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Monerans (bacteria) are prokaryotes, with DNA not enclosed in a nucleus.
quiz.explainWrong: Kingdom Monera is defined by the absence of a true nucleus — the other kingdoms are all eukaryotic.
quiz.narration: Which kingdom consists of organisms whose cells have no true nucleus?

quiz.question: Fungi are placed in their own kingdom, separate from plants, mainly because
options: fungi cannot photosynthesise and feed by absorption instead
fungi have no cell wall at all
fungi can move around freely like animals
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — fungi feed by releasing enzymes and absorbing nutrients, unlike photosynthesising plants.
quiz.explainWrong: Fungi lack chloroplasts and cannot photosynthesise; they absorb nutrients instead, which sets them apart from plants.
quiz.narration: Fungi are placed in their own kingdom, separate from plants, mainly because

quiz.question: A cell with a cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts most likely belongs to
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a cellulose wall and chloroplasts are defining features of plant cells.
quiz.explainWrong: A cellulose cell wall with chloroplasts is characteristic of Kingdom Plantae, not the other kingdoms.
quiz.narration: A cell with a cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts most likely belongs to

quiz.question: Organisms such as Amoeba and Paramecium, which are single-celled but have a true nucleus, belong to which kingdom?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Protists are mostly single-celled eukaryotes that don't fit into the other three multicellular kingdoms.
quiz.explainWrong: Amoeba and Paramecium are Protists — single-celled but with a true nucleus, unlike Monera.
quiz.narration: Organisms such as Amoeba and Paramecium, which are single-celled but have a true nucleus, belong to which kingdom?

stories.sub: A name every scientist on Earth agrees on
stories.heading: Binomial nomenclature
list: Before standard naming, a single species could have dozens of common names across different languages.
Linnaeus's binomial system gives every species exactly one two-word Latin name, used worldwide.
This is why scientific papers from Nigeria, Japan and Brazil can all refer to Panthera leo and mean the exact same lion.
stories.narration: Before standard naming, a single species could have dozens of common names across languages. Linnaeus's binomial system gives every species exactly one two-word Latin name, used worldwide, so scientists everywhere can refer to Panthera leo and mean the exact same lion.

stories.sub: How do you identify a mystery organism?
stories.heading: Twenty questions, biologist-style
list: Field biologists use identification keys — a structured series of either/or questions.
Each answer narrows down the possibilities until only one species remains.
This is the same logic as a 20-questions game, applied systematically to biology.
stories.narration: Field biologists use identification keys — a structured series of either/or questions. Each answer narrows down the possibilities until only one species remains, the same logic as a twenty-questions game applied systematically to biology.

lessons.heading: The rules of binomial nomenclature
list: Every species gets a two-part Latin name: Genus + species, e.g. Homo sapiens.
The genus name starts with a capital letter; the species name is all lowercase.
Both words are italicised when typed, or underlined when handwritten.
lessons.sub: Homo sapiens — capital Genus, lowercase species, always italicised.
lessons.narration: Every species gets a two-part Latin name: genus plus species, such as Homo sapiens. The genus name starts with a capital letter, the species name is lowercase, and both are italicised when typed or underlined when handwritten.

lessons.heading: One name, no confusion
list: Latin was chosen because it was the shared scientific language of Linnaeus's time and belongs to no single modern country.
A binomial name is unique to one species only, avoiding the confusion of local common names.
Example: what Nigerians may call ‘bush mango’ has one single scientific name recognised worldwide, Irvingia gabonensis.
lessons.sub: A scientific name has no ambiguity — a common name often does.
lessons.narration: Latin was chosen because it was the shared scientific language of Linnaeus's time and belongs to no single modern country. A binomial name is unique to one species, avoiding the confusion that local common names can cause.

lessons.heading: How a dichotomous key works
list: A dichotomous key presents a series of paired statements about an organism's features.
At each step, you choose the statement that fits, which either names the organism or sends you to the next pair.
‘Dichotomous’ means ‘divided into two’ — every step is a fork with exactly two branches.
lessons.sub: Each step is a fork in the road with only two paths.
lessons.narration: A dichotomous key presents a series of paired statements about an organism's features. At each step, you choose the statement that fits, which either names the organism or sends you to the next pair — dichotomous means divided into two.

lessons.heading: Using a simple key
list: 1a. Has wings — go to 2. 1b. Has no wings — it is a millipede.
2a. Has one pair of wings — it is a fly. 2b. Has two pairs of wings — it is a butterfly.
Following the fitting statement at each numbered step leads you to a final identification.
lessons.sub: Read each pair, pick the true one, follow where it sends you.
lessons.narration: For example: if the organism has wings, go to step two; if not, it is a millipede. At step two, one pair of wings means it is a fly, and two pairs of wings means it is a butterfly. Following the fitting statement at each step leads to a final identification.

lessons.heading: Common WAEC pitfalls on naming and keys
list: Do not capitalise the species name — only the genus name gets a capital letter.
Do not swap the order — genus always comes first, species always second.
When using a key in an exam, work through the pairs in order; don't guess or skip steps.
lessons.sub: Homo Sapiens and homo sapiens are both wrong formats — Homo sapiens is correct.
lessons.narration: Do not capitalise the species name — only the genus name gets a capital letter, and genus always comes first. When using a key in an exam, work through the numbered pairs in order rather than guessing.

quiz.question: In the scientific name Panthera leo, what does ‘Panthera’ represent?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the first word of a binomial name is always the genus.
quiz.explainWrong: ‘Panthera’ is the genus; ‘leo’ is the species — the genus is always written first.
quiz.narration: In the scientific name Panthera leo, what does ‘Panthera’ represent?

quiz.question: Which of these is correctly formatted as a scientific (binomial) name?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — genus capitalised, species lowercase, genus first: Homo sapiens.
quiz.explainWrong: The correct format capitalises only the genus, keeps the species lowercase, and puts genus first: Homo sapiens.
quiz.narration: Which of these is correctly formatted as a scientific (binomial) name?

quiz.question: A dichotomous key works by
options: presenting paired either/or statements that narrow down an identification step by step
showing only pictures with no text
requiring DNA testing at every step
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a dichotomous key is a series of two-choice steps that narrow down the identity of an organism.
quiz.explainWrong: A dichotomous key uses paired either/or statements at each step, not alphabetical lists or DNA testing.
quiz.narration: A dichotomous key works by

quiz.question: Why is binomial nomenclature preferred over common names in science?
options: Each species gets one unique name recognised worldwide, avoiding confusion
It is easier to say than any common name
It only applies to animals, not plants
It changes every year to stay current
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a scientific name is unique and globally standardised, unlike local common names.
quiz.explainWrong: Binomial names give each species one unique, globally recognised name — the benefit is avoiding the ambiguity of local common names.
quiz.narration: Why is binomial nomenclature preferred over common names in science?

topics.title: Diversity of Plants
topics.description: From simple algae to flowering trees — the four major plant groups and how they differ.

stories.sub: Life before roots and stems existed
stories.heading: The simplest plant-like organisms
list: Thallophytes were among the very first photosynthesising organisms — mostly aquatic algae.
Their whole body is a simple structure called a thallus, with no true root, stem or leaf.
Green pond scum, seaweed and Spirogyra are all everyday examples.
stories.narration: Thallophytes were among the very first photosynthesising organisms, mostly aquatic algae. Their whole body is a simple structure called a thallus, with no true root, stem or leaf — green pond scum, seaweed and Spirogyra are everyday examples.

stories.sub: Small, low, and never far from water
stories.heading: Why mosses stay tiny
list: Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts) were among the first plants to colonise land, but only partly succeeded.
They have no true vascular tissue to carry water upward, so they can't grow tall.
They also need a film of water on their surface for sperm to swim to the egg during reproduction — which is why mosses grow in damp, shady places.
stories.narration: Bryophytes, like mosses and liverworts, were among the first plants to colonise land, but only partly succeeded. They have no vascular tissue to carry water upward, so they can't grow tall, and they need a film of water for sperm to swim to the egg — which is why mosses grow in damp, shady places.

lessons.heading: Where these groups sit in plant diversity
list: Thallophyta (algae) and Bryophyta (mosses/liverworts) are the two simplest plant groups.
Neither group has true roots, stems or leaves, and neither produces flowers or seeds.
They reproduce mainly by spores, not seeds.
lessons.sub: Simplest body plan, no seeds, no flowers, no vascular tissue (in Thallophyta).
lessons.narration: Thallophyta, the algae, and Bryophyta, the mosses and liverworts, are the two simplest plant groups. Neither has true roots, stems or leaves, and neither produces flowers or seeds — they reproduce mainly by spores.

lessons.heading: Algae — body plan and habitat
list: The body is called a thallus: undifferentiated, with no separate root, stem or leaf.
Almost all thallophytes live in water or very damp places.
Examples: Spirogyra (freshwater, thread-like), Chlamydomonas (single-celled), seaweeds like kelp.
lessons.sub: A thallus is a plant body with no proper organs — just a simple mass or thread of cells.
lessons.narration: The algal body is called a thallus — undifferentiated, with no separate root, stem or leaf. Almost all thallophytes live in water or very damp places, examples including Spirogyra, Chlamydomonas and seaweeds.

lessons.heading: Mosses and liverworts — body plan and habitat
list: Bryophytes have simple leaf-like and stem-like parts, but no true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
They are anchored by root-like structures called rhizoids, not true roots.
They grow low and in clumps, typically in damp, shaded habitats like forest floors and riverbanks.
lessons.sub: Rhizoids anchor, but don't absorb water efficiently like true roots do.
lessons.narration: Bryophytes have simple leaf-like and stem-like parts, but no true vascular tissue. They are anchored by root-like structures called rhizoids, and typically grow low, in damp, shaded habitats.

lessons.heading: Spores, not seeds
list: Both groups reproduce using spores — tiny, light reproductive cells, not seeds.
Bryophytes need a film of surface water for the sperm to swim to the egg cell.
This water-dependence is the main reason bryophytes never colonised dry habitats successfully.
lessons.sub: No seed coat, no drought protection — spores need dampness to complete reproduction.
lessons.narration: Both groups reproduce using spores, not seeds. Bryophytes specifically need a film of surface water for the sperm to swim to the egg — which is the main reason bryophytes never colonised dry habitats successfully.

lessons.heading: Thallophyta vs Bryophyta — the quick test
list: Thallophyta: body is an undifferentiated thallus; almost always aquatic.
Bryophyta: has simple leaf-like/stem-like parts and rhizoids; mostly terrestrial but needs dampness.
Neither group has true vascular tissue, true roots, flowers or seeds — a favourite distractor in WAEC options.
lessons.sub: If an option says ‘has seeds’ or ‘has flowers’, it is NOT Thallophyta or Bryophyta.
lessons.narration: Thallophyta has an undifferentiated thallus and is almost always aquatic. Bryophyta has simple leaf-like and stem-like parts with rhizoids, and is mostly terrestrial but needs dampness. Neither group has true vascular tissue, roots, flowers or seeds.

quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a thallus is a plant body with no true root, stem or leaf.
quiz.explainWrong: The undifferentiated algal body is called a thallus, not a rhizoid, frond or sporophyte.
quiz.narration: The simple, undifferentiated body of an alga is called a
