quiz.explainWrong: Bryophytes are anchored by rhizoids, not true roots — a key feature separating them from higher plants.
quiz.narration: Mosses are anchored to their substrate by structures called

quiz.question: Why are mosses restricted to damp, shaded habitats?
options: Their sperm needs a film of water to swim to the egg cell
They cannot photosynthesise without direct sunlight
They only grow where there is no soil
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — bryophyte fertilisation depends on surface water for sperm to swim to the egg.
quiz.explainWrong: Mosses need damp conditions because their sperm must swim through a film of water to reach the egg cell.
quiz.narration: Why are mosses restricted to damp, shaded habitats?

quiz.question: Thallophyta and Bryophyta both reproduce mainly by
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — neither group produces seeds or flowers; both rely on spores.
quiz.explainWrong: Both groups reproduce by spores — neither has evolved seeds, flowers or fruits.
quiz.narration: Thallophyta and Bryophyta both reproduce mainly by

stories.sub: The upgrade that let plants grow tall
stories.heading: Ferns invented plant plumbing
list: Ferns were among the first plants to evolve true vascular tissue — xylem to carry water up, phloem to carry food around.
This ‘plumbing’ let ferns grow much larger than any moss ever could.
Fossil ferns from over 300 million years ago formed the giant swamp forests that became today's coal deposits.
stories.narration: Ferns were among the first plants to evolve true vascular tissue — xylem to carry water up, and phloem to carry food around. This plumbing let ferns grow much larger than any moss, and fossil ferns from over three hundred million years ago formed the giant swamp forests that became today's coal deposits.

stories.sub: An upgrade with one leftover weakness
stories.heading: Why ferns still need damp soil
list: Ferns solved the height problem with vascular tissue — but not the reproduction problem.
Like bryophytes, fern sperm must still swim through a film of water to reach the egg.
This is why ferns thrive in humid forests but are rare in deserts.
stories.narration: Ferns solved the height problem with vascular tissue, but not the reproduction problem — like bryophytes, fern sperm must still swim through a film of water to reach the egg, which is why ferns thrive in humid forests but are rare in deserts.

lessons.heading: What sets Pteridophyta apart
list: Pteridophytes have true roots, stems and leaves, unlike Thallophyta and Bryophyta.
They have true vascular tissue (xylem and phloem).
They still reproduce by spores, not seeds.
lessons.sub: True vascular tissue + true roots/stems/leaves, but still no seeds.
lessons.narration: Pteridophytes have true roots, stems and leaves, and true vascular tissue, unlike Thallophyta and Bryophyta — but they still reproduce by spores, not seeds.

lessons.heading: The parts of a fern
list: The leaf of a fern is called a frond; young fronds are tightly coiled, called fiddleheads.
Brown dot-like clusters on the underside of fronds, called sori, contain spore-producing structures.
The underground stem, called a rhizome, anchors the plant and produces new fronds each season.
lessons.sub: Frond = leaf. Sori = spore clusters. Rhizome = underground stem.
lessons.narration: The leaf of a fern is called a frond, and young fronds start tightly coiled, called fiddleheads. Brown dot-like clusters on the underside, called sori, contain spore-producing structures, while the underground stem, the rhizome, anchors the plant.

lessons.heading: Xylem and phloem — the plant's plumbing
list: Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals from roots upward through the plant.
Phloem transports the food made in photosynthesis to every part of the plant, including roots.
This is the first plant group in the syllabus to have both — that's what allows real height.
lessons.sub: Xylem moves water up; phloem moves food around.
lessons.narration: Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots. Phloem transports the food made in photosynthesis to every part of the plant, including the roots. This is the first plant group with both, which is what allows real height.

lessons.heading: The fern life cycle in brief
list: Mature fronds release spores from the sori; spores that land in a damp spot grow into a small, flat structure called a prothallus.
The prothallus produces sperm and egg cells; the sperm swims through water to fertilise the egg.
The fertilised egg grows into a new, familiar-looking fern plant.
lessons.sub: Spore → prothallus → fertilisation (needs water) → new fern.
lessons.narration: Mature fronds release spores from the sori. A spore that lands in a damp spot grows into a small, flat structure called a prothallus, which produces sperm and egg cells. The sperm swims through water to fertilise the egg, which then grows into a new fern.

lessons.heading: Pteridophyta's defining combination
list: True roots, stems, leaves AND true vascular tissue — but reproduces by spores, not seeds.
This combination (vascular but no seeds) is unique to Pteridophyta in the plant kingdom.
WAEC often tests this exact contrast: ‘vascular but seedless’ = ferns.
lessons.sub: Vascular + seedless is the unique fingerprint of Pteridophyta.
lessons.narration: The defining combination is true roots, stems, leaves and true vascular tissue, but reproduction by spores, not seeds — vascular but seedless is unique to Pteridophyta, and a combination WAEC often tests directly.

quiz.question: What is the main feature that separates Pteridophyta from Thallophyta and Bryophyta?
options: Pteridophytes have true vascular tissue (xylem and phloem)
Pteridophytes have no leaves at all
Pteridophytes live only in the ocean
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — true vascular tissue is the key upgrade Pteridophyta has over the two simpler groups.
quiz.explainWrong: The key difference is true vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) — Pteridophytes don't produce flowers.
quiz.narration: What is the main feature that separates Pteridophyta from Thallophyta and Bryophyta?

quiz.question: The brown, dot-like clusters found on the underside of a fern frond are called
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — sori are clusters containing the fern's spore-producing structures.
quiz.explainWrong: These clusters are called sori — the rhizome is the underground stem, not a surface structure.
quiz.narration: The brown, dot-like clusters found on the underside of a fern frond are called

quiz.question: In a fern's vascular tissue, which of these correctly describes xylem's function?
options: Transports water and dissolved minerals from the roots upward
Transports food made in photosynthesis to the roots
Anchors the fern to the soil
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — xylem carries water and minerals upward; phloem carries food.
quiz.explainWrong: Xylem's job is transporting water and minerals upward from the roots — transporting food is phloem's job.
quiz.narration: In a fern's vascular tissue, which of these correctly describes xylem's function?

quiz.question: Like mosses, ferns still require water for reproduction because
options: fern sperm must swim through a film of water to reach the egg
fern spores cannot survive without constant water
fern roots cannot absorb water without help
fern leaves dissolve in dry air
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — despite having vascular tissue, ferns retained a bryophyte-like need for water during fertilisation.
quiz.explainWrong: Fern sperm still needs a film of water to swim to the egg cell — vascular tissue solved height, not reproduction.
quiz.narration: Like mosses, ferns still require water for reproduction because

stories.sub: A survival capsule for the next generation
stories.heading: The invention of the seed
list: The seed was a breakthrough: an embryo plant packaged with its own food supply, protected by a tough coat.
Unlike a spore, a seed can survive drought, cold, and being buried, waiting until conditions are right to germinate.
Seed plants no longer need water for fertilisation — pollen replaced swimming sperm.
stories.narration: The seed was a breakthrough: an embryo plant packaged with its own food supply, protected by a tough coat. Unlike a spore, a seed can survive drought and cold, waiting until conditions are right — and seed plants no longer need water for fertilisation, because pollen replaced swimming sperm.

stories.sub: Naked seeds vs seeds inside a fruit
stories.heading: Pine cones and flowers took different paths
list: Gymnosperms (e.g. pine trees) produce ‘naked’ seeds, exposed on the scales of cones.
Angiosperms (flowering plants) enclose their seeds inside a protective fruit, developed from the flower's ovary.
Angiosperms are now the most successful and diverse plant group on Earth, from grasses to oak trees.
stories.narration: Gymnosperms, like pine trees, produce naked seeds, exposed on the scales of cones. Angiosperms, the flowering plants, enclose their seeds inside a protective fruit, and are now the most successful and diverse plant group on Earth.

lessons.heading: What makes Spermatophyta the most advanced group
list: Spermatophyta means ‘seed plants’ — they reproduce by seeds, not spores.
They have true roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue, like Pteridophyta, plus the seed upgrade.
They are split into two groups: Gymnosperms (naked seeds) and Angiosperms (flowering plants).
lessons.sub: Spermatophyta = vascular plants that make seeds.
lessons.narration: Spermatophyta means seed plants — they reproduce by seeds, not spores, and have true roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue. They split into two groups: Gymnosperms with naked seeds, and Angiosperms, the flowering plants.

lessons.heading: Naked-seed plants
list: ‘Gymnosperm’ means ‘naked seed’ — the seed is not enclosed in a fruit.
Seeds develop exposed on the surface of scales, usually arranged into a cone.
Examples: pine, cypress, and other cone-bearing (coniferous) trees.
lessons.sub: No fruit wrapper — the seed sits exposed on a cone scale.
lessons.narration: Gymnosperm means naked seed — the seed is not enclosed in a fruit, but develops exposed on the surface of a cone's scales, as in pine and other coniferous trees.

lessons.heading: Flowering plants
list: ‘Angiosperm’ means ‘seed in a vessel’ — the seed develops enclosed inside a fruit.
Angiosperms produce flowers, the reproductive structure that develops into fruit after fertilisation.
They are divided into monocotyledons and dicotyledons, based on the number of seed leaves in the embryo.
lessons.sub: Flower → fertilisation → fruit, with seeds protected inside.
lessons.narration: Angiosperm means seed in a vessel — the seed develops enclosed inside a fruit. Angiosperms produce flowers, and are divided into monocotyledons and dicotyledons, based on the number of seed leaves in the embryo.

lessons.heading: Telling the two angiosperm groups apart
list: Monocotyledons: one seed leaf (cotyledon), parallel leaf veins, fibrous roots. Example: maize, rice, grasses.
Dicotyledons: two seed leaves, net-like (branching) leaf veins, a tap root. Example: beans, mango, hibiscus.
Flower parts are also a clue: monocots often have parts in multiples of 3; dicots in multiples of 4 or 5.
lessons.sub: One seed leaf + parallel veins = monocot. Two seed leaves + net veins = dicot.
lessons.narration: Monocotyledons have one seed leaf, parallel leaf veins and fibrous roots, as in maize and rice. Dicotyledons have two seed leaves, net-like leaf veins and a tap root, as in beans and mango.

lessons.heading: The full plant hierarchy, top to bottom
list: Thallophyta (no vascular tissue, no roots/stems/leaves) → Bryophyta (simple parts, no vascular tissue) → Pteridophyta (vascular, spores) → Spermatophyta (vascular, seeds).
Within Spermatophyta: Gymnosperms (naked seed, cones) and Angiosperms (seed in fruit, flowers).
Within Angiosperms: Monocotyledons (1 seed leaf) and Dicotyledons (2 seed leaves).
lessons.sub: Learn this ladder — WAEC tests it as a complete sequence, not isolated facts.
lessons.narration: The full ladder runs: Thallophyta, then Bryophyta, then Pteridophyta with vascular tissue and spores, then Spermatophyta with vascular tissue and seeds — splitting into Gymnosperms and Angiosperms, and Angiosperms splitting again into monocotyledons and dicotyledons.

quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — ‘Spermatophyta’ means seed plants, unlike the spore-producing Pteridophyta.
quiz.explainWrong: Spermatophyta reproduce by seeds; Pteridophyta (ferns) reproduce by spores.

quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Gymnosperm literally means ‘naked seed’.
quiz.explainWrong: Naked, cone-exposed seeds are the defining feature of Gymnosperms, not Angiosperms.

quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — one seed leaf and parallel veins are classic monocotyledon features, as in maize.
quiz.explainWrong: One seed leaf with parallel veins describes a monocotyledon — dicots have two seed leaves and net veins.

quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Spermatophyta is the correct order of increasing complexity.
quiz.explainWrong: The correct order, simplest to most advanced, is Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, then Spermatophyta.

topics.title: Diversity of Animals
topics.description: From single-celled Amoeba to backboned mammals — the major invertebrate and vertebrate groups.

stories.sub: 97% of all animal species
stories.heading: Most animals aren't what you think
list: When people imagine ‘animals’, they usually picture backboned ones — but invertebrates make up about 97% of all animal species.
Invertebrates range from single-celled Amoeba to complex-bodied insects and octopuses.
This sub-topic covers the simplest invertebrate phyla, ordered roughly by increasing body complexity.
stories.narration: When people imagine animals, they usually picture backboned ones, but invertebrates make up about ninety-seven percent of all animal species, ranging from single-celled Amoeba to complex insects and octopuses.

stories.sub: Biology with real medical stakes
stories.heading: Why flatworms and roundworms matter in West Africa
list: Platyhelminthes (flatworms) include tapeworms and the parasite that causes schistosomiasis (bilharzia).
Nematodes (roundworms) include species that cause elephantiasis and intestinal worm infections.
Understanding these phyla isn't just exam content — it's directly relevant to public health.
stories.narration: Platyhelminthes, the flatworms, include tapeworms and the parasite that causes schistosomiasis. Nematodes, the roundworms, include species that cause elephantiasis and intestinal worm infections — understanding these phyla is directly relevant to public health, not just exams.

lessons.heading: Invertebrates — animals without a backbone
list: Invertebrates are animals with no vertebral column (backbone).
They are grouped into phyla based on body plan: symmetry, body cavity, and level of organisation.
This sub-topic covers five simpler phyla: Protozoa, Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes and Nematoda.
lessons.sub: No backbone = invertebrate. That's the entire test.
lessons.narration: Invertebrates are animals with no vertebral column, grouped into phyla based on body plan. This sub-topic covers five simpler phyla: Protozoa, Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes and Nematoda.

lessons.heading: Single-celled animals
list: Protozoa are single-celled organisms that behave like tiny animals: they move and feed on other organisms.
Examples: Amoeba (moves using flowing pseudopodia), Paramecium (moves using tiny hair-like cilia).
Plasmodium, the malaria parasite, is also a protozoan.
lessons.sub: One cell, but a full life: moving, feeding, reproducing.
lessons.narration: Protozoa are single-celled organisms that move and feed like tiny animals. Amoeba moves using flowing pseudopodia, Paramecium uses tiny hair-like cilia, and Plasmodium, the malaria parasite, is also a protozoan.

lessons.heading: Sponges and stinging animals
list: Porifera (sponges) have a body full of pores, with no true tissues or organs — the simplest true multicellular animals.
Coelenterata (e.g. Hydra, jellyfish, coral) have a sac-like body with one opening and stinging cells called cnidocytes.
Both groups show radial symmetry — their body parts are arranged around a central axis.
lessons.sub: Pores with no tissues = sponge. Sac body with stinging cells = coelenterate.
lessons.narration: Porifera, the sponges, have a body full of pores with no true tissues or organs. Coelenterata, like Hydra and jellyfish, have a sac-like body with one opening and stinging cells called cnidocytes. Both show radial symmetry.

lessons.heading: Flatworms
list: Platyhelminthes have flattened, ribbon-like bodies with bilateral symmetry (a distinct left and right side).
Many are parasitic: tapeworms live in the gut; Schistosoma causes schistosomiasis (bilharzia).
They have no true body cavity and no circulatory system — nutrients simply diffuse through the flat body.
lessons.sub: Flat body = short diffusion distance, which is why they don't need a circulatory system.
lessons.narration: Platyhelminthes, the flatworms, have flattened, ribbon-like bodies with bilateral symmetry. Many are parasitic — tapeworms live in the gut, and Schistosoma causes schistosomiasis. They have no circulatory system; nutrients simply diffuse through the flat body.

lessons.heading: Roundworms
list: Nematodes have a cylindrical, unsegmented body, pointed at both ends.
Unlike Platyhelminthes, they have a complete digestive tract with two openings (mouth and anus).
Examples: Ascaris (intestinal roundworm), Wuchereria (causes elephantiasis).
lessons.sub: Round in cross-section, pointed at both ends, tube-within-a-tube gut.
lessons.narration: Nematodes have a cylindrical, unsegmented body, pointed at both ends, with a complete digestive tract that has both a mouth and an anus — unlike flatworms. Examples include Ascaris and Wuchereria, which causes elephantiasis.

quiz.question: Amoeba and Paramecium, which move and feed like tiny animals despite being single-celled, belong to phylum
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Protozoa are single-celled organisms that behave like tiny animals.
quiz.explainWrong: Amoeba and Paramecium are Protozoa — single-celled but showing animal-like movement and feeding.
quiz.narration: Amoeba and Paramecium, which move and feed like tiny animals despite being single-celled, belong to phylum

quiz.question: A sac-like body with one opening and stinging cells (cnidocytes), as in Hydra, is characteristic of phylum
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — stinging cells (cnidocytes) and a sac-like single-opening body are defining Coelenterata features.
quiz.explainWrong: Cnidocytes and a sac-like body with one opening describe Coelenterata, not Porifera or the other phyla.
quiz.narration: A sac-like body with one opening and stinging cells (cnidocytes), as in Hydra, is characteristic of phylum

quiz.question: Tapeworms and Schistosoma, the parasite that causes schistosomiasis, belong to phylum
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — flatworms (Platyhelminthes) include tapeworms and Schistosoma.
quiz.explainWrong: Tapeworms and Schistosoma are Platyhelminthes (flatworms), not roundworms or coelenterates.
quiz.narration: Tapeworms and Schistosoma, the parasite that causes schistosomiasis, belong to phylum

quiz.question: Which feature distinguishes Nematoda from Platyhelminthes?
options: Nematodes have a complete digestive tract with both a mouth and an anus
Nematodes have no digestive tract at all
Nematodes are always free-living, never parasitic
Nematodes have a flattened, ribbon-like body
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Nematodes have a complete gut with two openings; Platyhelminthes have only one opening.
quiz.explainWrong: Nematodes have a complete digestive tract with a mouth and an anus — Platyhelminthes have only one gut opening.
quiz.narration: Which feature distinguishes Nematoda from Platyhelminthes?

stories.sub: One phylum, over a million known species
stories.heading: Arthropods rule the planet
list: Phylum Arthropoda contains more known species than every other animal phylum combined.
Insects alone make up roughly three-quarters of all known animal species on Earth.
Their secret weapon: a tough, lightweight exoskeleton and jointed limbs adaptable to almost any habitat.
stories.narration: Phylum Arthropoda contains more known species than every other animal phylum combined — insects alone make up roughly three-quarters of all known animal species. Their secret is a tough, lightweight exoskeleton and jointed limbs adaptable to almost any habitat.

stories.sub: Why earthworms are good for soil
stories.heading: The value of a segmented body
list: Phylum Annelida (segmented worms) includes earthworms, which constantly burrow through and aerate soil.
Charles Darwin spent decades studying earthworms, calling them one of the most important creatures in Earth's history.
Their segmented body plan let each section specialise slightly — an evolutionary innovation echoed in insects and even humans (our segmented spine).
stories.narration: Phylum Annelida, the segmented worms, includes earthworms, which constantly burrow through and aerate soil. Charles Darwin spent decades studying earthworms, calling them one of the most important creatures in Earth's history.

lessons.heading: Segmented worms
list: Annelids have a body divided into repeating ring-like segments.
Each segment can contain its own set of muscles, nerves and excretory structures.
Examples: earthworm (Lumbricus), leech.
lessons.sub: Segments = the body plan upgrade over simple worms.
lessons.narration: Annelids have a body divided into repeating ring-like segments, each with its own muscles, nerves and excretory structures — examples include the earthworm and the leech.

lessons.heading: Jointed-leg animals
list: Arthropods have a hard external skeleton (exoskeleton) made of chitin, and jointed limbs.

The phylum is split into classes: Insecta (3 body parts, 3 pairs of legs, e.g. housefly), Arachnida (2 body parts, 4 pairs of legs, e.g. spider), Crustacea (e.g. crab), Myriapoda (e.g. millipede, centipede — many segments, many legs).
The exoskeleton must be periodically shed (moulting) for the animal to grow.
lessons.sub: Exoskeleton + jointed legs = Arthropoda. Count the legs to find the class.
lessons.narration: Arthropods have a hard chitin exoskeleton and jointed limbs. The phylum splits into classes: Insecta with three body parts and three pairs of legs, Arachnida with two body parts and four pairs of legs, Crustacea like crabs, and Myriapoda like millipedes and centipedes.

lessons.heading: Soft-bodied animals
list: Molluscs have a soft, unsegmented body, often protected by a hard shell made of calcium carbonate.
Most move using a muscular foot.
Examples: snail (shelled), octopus (shell reduced/absent), slug, oyster.
lessons.sub: Soft body + muscular foot, usually with a shell.
lessons.narration: Molluscs have a soft, unsegmented body, often protected by a hard calcium carbonate shell, and most move using a muscular foot — examples include the snail, octopus, slug and oyster.

lessons.heading: Spiny-skinned, five-part animals
list: Echinoderms show five-part radial symmetry as adults (think of a starfish's five arms).
Their skin contains hard, spiny plates made of calcium carbonate, just beneath the surface.
Examples: starfish, sea urchin, brittle star — all marine, none live on land or in freshwater.
lessons.sub: Five-part body plan + spiny skin + always marine.
lessons.narration: Echinoderms show five-part radial symmetry as adults, like a starfish's five arms, with hard spiny plates just beneath the skin — examples include starfish and sea urchins, and all are marine.

lessons.heading: Telling the advanced invertebrate phyla apart
list: Segmented, soft body, no shell → Annelida.
Exoskeleton + jointed legs → Arthropoda (count legs/body parts for the class).
Soft body + muscular foot (often shelled) → Mollusca. Five-part spiny marine body → Echinodermata.
lessons.sub: Four quick checks: segments, exoskeleton+legs, foot+shell, or five-part spiny.
lessons.narration: A segmented, soft, unshelled body is Annelida. An exoskeleton with jointed legs is Arthropoda. A soft body with a muscular foot, often shelled, is Mollusca. A five-part, spiny, marine body is Echinodermata.

quiz.question: A body divided into repeating ring-like segments, as seen in the earthworm, is characteristic of phylum
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Annelida (segmented worms) have a body of repeating ring-like segments.
quiz.explainWrong: Repeating ring-like segments describe Annelida — Arthropoda has jointed limbs and an exoskeleton instead.
quiz.narration: A body divided into repeating ring-like segments, as seen in the earthworm, is characteristic of phylum

quiz.question: Insects, spiders and crabs are all grouped in phylum Arthropoda mainly because they share
options: a hard exoskeleton and jointed limbs
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a chitin exoskeleton with jointed limbs is the defining feature of Arthropoda.
quiz.explainWrong: Arthropods share a hard exoskeleton and jointed limbs — not a soft shelled body or radial symmetry.
quiz.narration: Insects, spiders and crabs are all grouped in phylum Arthropoda mainly because they share

quiz.question: A snail's soft body, protected by a spiral shell and moved by a muscular foot, places it in phylum
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a soft body with a muscular foot, often shelled, is characteristic of Mollusca.
quiz.explainWrong: A soft, shelled body moved by a muscular foot describes Mollusca, not Annelida or Arthropoda.
quiz.narration: A snail's soft body, protected by a spiral shell and moved by a muscular foot, places it in phylum

quiz.question: The starfish shows five-part radial symmetry and spiny skin plates, placing it in phylum
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — five-part radial symmetry and spiny skin plates are the hallmark of Echinodermata.
quiz.explainWrong: Five-part radial symmetry with spiny plates describes Echinodermata, all of which are marine animals.
quiz.narration: The starfish shows five-part radial symmetry and spiny skin plates, placing it in phylum

stories.sub: Rare, but familiar
stories.heading: Why vertebrates feel so central to biology
list: Vertebrates make up only about 3% of animal species — yet they dominate biology textbooks and everyday attention.
That's likely because humans are vertebrates, and we find backboned animals easiest to relate to.
All vertebrates share one defining feature: a vertebral column (backbone) protecting a dorsal nerve cord.
stories.narration: Vertebrates make up only about three percent of animal species, yet they dominate biology textbooks — likely because humans are vertebrates ourselves. All vertebrates share one defining feature: a vertebral column protecting a dorsal nerve cord.

stories.sub: Same blueprint, different habitats
stories.heading: How one ancestor became fish, frogs and elephants
list: All five vertebrate classes evolved from a shared fish-like ancestor over hundreds of millions of years.
Each class represents a different solution to living in water, on land, or both.
Comparing them side by side is one of the clearest illustrations of evolution in the whole syllabus.
stories.narration: All five vertebrate classes evolved from a shared fish-like ancestor over hundreds of millions of years, each representing a different solution to living in water, on land, or both — one of the clearest illustrations of evolution in the whole syllabus.

lessons.heading: What makes an animal a vertebrate
list: Vertebrates have a vertebral column (backbone) made of individual vertebrae, protecting the spinal cord.
They also have an internal skeleton (endoskeleton), unlike the exoskeleton of arthropods.
There are five classes: Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia.
lessons.sub: Backbone + internal skeleton = vertebrate.
lessons.narration: Vertebrates have a vertebral column made of individual vertebrae, protecting the spinal cord, and an internal skeleton unlike the exoskeleton of arthropods. There are five classes: Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia.

lessons.heading: Fish — the original vertebrates
list: Fish breathe using gills and live their entire life in water.
Their skin is usually covered in scales, and most have fins for swimming.
Most fish are ectothermic (‘cold-blooded’) — their body temperature matches their surroundings.
lessons.sub: Gills + scales + fins + water-only life = Pisces.
lessons.narration: Fish breathe using gills and live their entire life in water. Their skin is usually covered in scales, and most have fins for swimming — and most fish are ectothermic, meaning their body temperature matches their surroundings.

lessons.heading: The land-and-water in-betweeners, and true land dwellers
list: Amphibians (e.g. frogs, toads) live a double life: gills and water as larvae (tadpoles), lungs and skin breathing as adults — and must return to water to breed.
Reptiles (e.g. lizards, snakes) have dry, scaly skin that resists water loss, and lay shelled eggs on land — a big step toward full independence from water.
Both classes are ectothermic, like fish.
lessons.sub: Amphibian = needs water to breed. Reptile = dry scales, shelled eggs on land.
lessons.narration: Amphibians live a double life — gills and water as tadpoles, lungs as adults — and must return to water to breed. Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and lay shelled eggs on land, a big step toward independence from water. Both classes are ectothermic.

lessons.heading: The warm-blooded classes
list: Birds (Aves) have feathers, forelimbs modified into wings, and lay hard-shelled eggs.
Mammals (Mammalia) have hair or fur, feed their young on milk from mammary glands, and (with two rare exceptions) give birth to live young.
Both classes are endothermic (‘warm-blooded’) — they generate and regulate their own body heat.
lessons.sub: Feathers + wings = Aves. Hair + milk = Mammalia. Both keep their own body heat.
lessons.narration: Birds have feathers, wings, and lay hard-shelled eggs. Mammals have hair or fur, feed their young on milk, and mostly give birth to live young. Both classes are endothermic, generating and regulating their own body heat.

lessons.heading: The five-class comparison table
list: Pisces: gills, scales, water only, ectothermic. Amphibia: gills then lungs, needs water to breed, ectothermic.
Reptilia: lungs, dry scales, shelled eggs on land, ectothermic. Aves: lungs, feathers, hard-shelled eggs, endothermic.
Mammalia: lungs, hair/fur, milk from mammary glands, mostly live young, endothermic.
lessons.sub: ‘Ectothermic’ or ‘endothermic’ + breathing method is often the fastest way to identify the class in an exam.
lessons.narration: Pisces breathe by gills, are covered in scales and are ectothermic. Amphibia start with gills and end with lungs, needing water to breed. Reptilia have dry scales and shelled eggs on land. Aves have feathers and are endothermic. Mammalia have hair, feed on milk, and are endothermic.

quiz.question: What single feature defines all vertebrates?
options: A vertebral column (backbone) protecting the spinal cord
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a backbone protecting the spinal cord is the one feature shared by every vertebrate class.
quiz.explainWrong: Only a vertebral column protecting the spinal cord is shared by all vertebrates — not flight, warm-bloodedness or land life.
quiz.narration: What single feature defines all vertebrates?

quiz.question: An animal that starts life breathing with gills in water, then develops lungs as an adult but must return to water to breed, is a
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — this gills-then-lungs, water-dependent-breeding life cycle is characteristic of amphibians.
quiz.explainWrong: This double life — gills then lungs, breeding in water — describes Amphibia, not Pisces or Reptilia.
quiz.narration: An animal that starts life breathing with gills in water, then develops lungs as an adult but must return to water to breed, is a

quiz.question: Dry, scaly skin and shelled eggs laid on land, without needing to return to water, are typical of
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — dry scales and land-laid shelled eggs are the reptile solution to independence from water.
quiz.explainWrong: Dry scaly skin with shelled eggs laid on land describes Reptilia — amphibians must still return to water to breed.
quiz.narration: Dry, scaly skin and shelled eggs laid on land, without needing to return to water, are typical of

quiz.question: Which pair of classes are both endothermic (‘warm-blooded’)?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — Aves (birds) and Mammalia (mammals) generate and regulate their own body heat.
quiz.explainWrong: Only Aves and Mammalia are endothermic — Pisces, Amphibia and Reptilia are all ectothermic.
quiz.narration: Which pair of classes are both endothermic (‘warm-blooded’)?

topics.title: Nutrition in Plants
topics.description: How plants make their own food from sunlight, and how they get the minerals they can't make themselves.

stories.sub: Every meal you've ever eaten traces back to this
stories.heading: The reaction that feeds the planet
list: Almost every food chain on Earth begins with photosynthesis — plants capturing light energy and turning it into food.
The oxygen you're breathing right now was very likely released by a plant during photosynthesis.
It is, arguably, the single most important chemical reaction on the planet.
stories.narration: Almost every food chain on Earth begins with photosynthesis — plants capturing light energy and turning it into food. The oxygen you're breathing right now was very likely released by a plant during this exact reaction.

stories.sub: A plant in a jar, a mouse, and a candle
stories.heading: How Joseph Priestley discovered plants ‘purify’ air
list: Joseph Priestley found that a mouse or candle in a sealed jar would soon die out or go out.
But if a living plant was placed in the same sealed jar, the mouse survived and the candle kept burning longer.
He had discovered, without yet knowing the full chemistry, that plants release oxygen.
stories.narration: Joseph Priestley found that a mouse or candle sealed in a jar would soon die out or go out. But if a living plant was placed in the same jar, the mouse survived and the candle burned longer — he had discovered that plants release oxygen.

lessons.heading: What is photosynthesis?
list: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food using light energy.
It happens mainly in the leaf, inside cells containing the green pigment chlorophyll.
Word equation: carbon dioxide + water --(light energy, chlorophyll)--> glucose + oxygen.
lessons.sub: Sunlight + CO2 + water, trapped by chlorophyll, becomes sugar + oxygen.
lessons.narration: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food using light energy, mainly in leaf cells containing chlorophyll. Carbon dioxide plus water, with light energy and chlorophyll, produces glucose plus oxygen.

lessons.heading: The leaf as a food factory
list: Chloroplasts, containing chlorophyll, are concentrated in the palisade mesophyll layer near the leaf's upper surface.
Tiny pores called stomata (mostly on the leaf's underside) let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.
A network of veins (vascular bundles) delivers water in and carries glucose away.
lessons.sub: Chloroplasts trap light; stomata handle gas exchange; veins handle transport.
lessons.narration: Chloroplasts are concentrated in the palisade mesophyll layer near the leaf's upper surface. Tiny pores called stomata let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out, while a network of veins delivers water in and carries glucose away.

lessons.heading: The essential raw materials
list: Carbon dioxide — absorbed from air through the stomata.
Water — absorbed from soil by the roots, transported up via xylem.
Light energy — absorbed by chlorophyll, usually from sunlight.
lessons.sub: Remove any one of these three, and photosynthesis stops.
lessons.narration: Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide absorbed through the stomata, water absorbed from soil through the roots, and light energy absorbed by chlorophyll — remove any one of the three and the reaction stops.

lessons.heading: What happens to the glucose made?
list: Some glucose is used immediately for respiration, to release energy for the plant's own activities.
Some is converted to starch for storage — the standard test for photosynthesis is testing a leaf for starch.
Some is converted into cellulose (for cell walls), or combined with minerals to build proteins and other compounds.
lessons.sub: Glucose → used now (respiration), stored (starch), or built into the plant (cellulose, proteins).
lessons.narration: Some glucose is used immediately for respiration; some is converted to starch for storage, which is why testing a leaf for starch is the standard test for photosynthesis; and some is built into cellulose or, combined with minerals, into proteins.

lessons.heading: Factors that limit the rate of photosynthesis
list: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, and temperature can each become a ‘limiting factor’.
A limiting factor is whichever one of these is in shortest supply — increasing it speeds up the reaction; increasing the others makes no difference until that factor improves.
WAEC often shows a graph and asks which factor limits the rate at a given point.
lessons.sub: The scarcest factor sets the pace — like the slowest runner in a relay team.
lessons.narration: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature can each become a limiting factor — whichever is in shortest supply sets the pace of the reaction, no matter how much of the other two are available.

quiz.question: Which gas is absorbed by a plant during photosynthesis?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — carbon dioxide is absorbed through the stomata and combined with water to make glucose.
quiz.explainWrong: Photosynthesis absorbs carbon dioxide, not oxygen — oxygen is released as a product, not taken in.
quiz.narration: Which gas is absorbed by a plant during photosynthesis?

quiz.question: In which leaf cell layer are most chloroplasts concentrated?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the palisade mesophyll, near the leaf's upper surface, contains the most chloroplasts.
quiz.explainWrong: Chloroplasts are concentrated in the palisade mesophyll, not in the lower epidermis, xylem, or root cells.
quiz.narration: In which leaf cell layer are most chloroplasts concentrated?

quiz.question: The standard test to show that photosynthesis has occurred in a leaf checks for the presence of
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — glucose made in photosynthesis is quickly converted to starch for storage, which is what the iodine test detects.
quiz.explainWrong: The standard leaf test checks for starch, since glucose is rapidly converted to starch for storage.
quiz.narration: The standard test to show that photosynthesis has occurred in a leaf checks for the presence of

quiz.question: What is meant by a ‘limiting factor’ in photosynthesis?
options: Whichever factor is in shortest supply, setting the pace of the reaction
A factor that stops photosynthesis permanently
Any factor not needed for the reaction
The total amount of chlorophyll present
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — a limiting factor is the scarcest of light, CO2 or temperature, which caps the rate regardless of the others.
quiz.explainWrong: A limiting factor is the factor in shortest supply, capping the reaction rate — not a permanent stopper or unrelated variable.
quiz.narration: What is meant by a ‘limiting factor’ in photosynthesis?

stories.sub: Photosynthesis alone isn't enough
stories.heading: Why plants still need soil nutrients
list: Photosynthesis gives a plant energy-rich glucose — but glucose alone can't build every part of a plant.
Proteins, chlorophyll and DNA all require extra elements like nitrogen, magnesium and phosphorus.
Plants absorb these as dissolved mineral ions through their roots.
stories.narration: Photosynthesis gives a plant energy-rich glucose, but glucose alone can't build every part of a plant. Proteins, chlorophyll and DNA all require extra elements like nitrogen, magnesium and phosphorus, absorbed as dissolved mineral ions through the roots.

stories.sub: A plant's version of a food-deficiency disease
stories.heading: Yellow leaves are a cry for help
list: Farmers can often diagnose a mineral deficiency just by looking at leaf colour and growth pattern.
Pale yellow leaves often mean nitrogen or magnesium deficiency — both are needed to make chlorophyll.
This is why fertiliser exists: to replace minerals that crops remove from the soil each season.
stories.narration: Farmers can often diagnose a mineral deficiency just by looking at leaf colour and growth pattern. Pale yellow leaves often mean nitrogen or magnesium deficiency, since both are needed to make chlorophyll — which is exactly why fertiliser exists.

lessons.heading: Mineral ions plants absorb from soil
list: Plants absorb dissolved mineral ions from soil water through root hair cells.
Needed in relatively large amounts: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium.
Root hairs give roots a huge surface area for absorbing water and these minerals efficiently.
lessons.sub: Root hairs = the plant's mineral-absorbing surface.
lessons.narration: Plants absorb dissolved mineral ions from soil water through root hair cells, which give roots a huge surface area for absorbing water and minerals like nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium.

lessons.heading: Why nitrogen matters most
list: Nitrogen is needed to make proteins, chlorophyll, and DNA.
Deficiency symptom: stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves (chlorosis).
Nitrogen is absorbed mainly as nitrate ions.
lessons.sub: No nitrogen, no protein, no chlorophyll — the plant can't grow or stay green.
lessons.narration: Nitrogen is needed to make proteins, chlorophyll and DNA, and is absorbed mainly as nitrate ions. A nitrogen deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves.

lessons.heading: Two more essential minerals
list: Magnesium is a core component of the chlorophyll molecule itself — deficiency causes yellowing between leaf veins.
Phosphorus is needed for healthy root growth and for energy transfer within cells.
Phosphorus deficiency shows as poor root development and stunted, sometimes purplish, leaves.
lessons.sub: Magnesium builds chlorophyll directly; phosphorus fuels roots and energy transfer.
lessons.narration: Magnesium is a core part of the chlorophyll molecule itself, so its deficiency causes yellowing between leaf veins. Phosphorus is needed for healthy root growth and energy transfer, and its deficiency shows as poor roots and stunted, sometimes purplish, leaves.

lessons.heading: Fertilisers replace what crops remove
list: Every harvest removes minerals from the soil, locked inside the harvested plant material.
Fertilisers (organic, like manure and compost, or inorganic, like NPK fertiliser) return these minerals to the soil.
‘NPK’ fertiliser is named for its three main minerals: Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium.
lessons.sub: NPK = Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium — the big three replaced by fertiliser.
lessons.narration: Every harvest removes minerals from the soil, locked inside the harvested plant material. Fertilisers return these minerals — NPK fertiliser is named for its three main minerals: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

lessons.heading: Matching deficiency symptoms to minerals
list: General yellowing of older leaves + stunted growth → nitrogen deficiency.
Yellowing between the veins specifically → magnesium deficiency.
Poor root growth + stunted, purplish leaves → phosphorus deficiency.
lessons.sub: WAEC loves matching a described symptom to the missing mineral — learn these three patterns.
lessons.narration: Nitrogen deficiency shows as general yellowing of older leaves with stunted growth. Magnesium deficiency shows as yellowing specifically between the veins. Phosphorus deficiency shows as poor root growth and stunted, purplish leaves.

quiz.question: Root hairs increase a root's efficiency mainly by
options: increasing the surface area available for absorbing water and minerals
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — root hairs greatly increase surface area for water and mineral absorption.
quiz.explainWrong: Root hairs increase surface area for absorption — they don't photosynthesise or make chlorophyll.
quiz.narration: Root hairs increase a root's efficiency mainly by

quiz.question: A plant with stunted growth and yellowing of its older leaves most likely lacks
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — nitrogen deficiency shows as stunted growth with yellowing (chlorosis) of older leaves.
quiz.explainWrong: Stunted growth with yellowing older leaves is the classic nitrogen deficiency symptom, not phosphorus.
quiz.narration: A plant with stunted growth and yellowing of its older leaves most likely lacks

quiz.question: Which mineral is a direct component of the chlorophyll molecule itself?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — magnesium is a structural component of chlorophyll; its deficiency causes yellowing between veins.
quiz.explainWrong: Magnesium is built directly into the chlorophyll molecule — phosphorus and potassium play different roles.
quiz.narration: Which mineral is a direct component of the chlorophyll molecule itself?

quiz.question: In ‘NPK’ fertiliser, what does the ‘P’ stand for?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — NPK stands for Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium.
quiz.explainWrong: In NPK fertiliser, P stands for Phosphorus — K stands for Potassium, which is a separate letter.
quiz.narration: In ‘NPK’ fertiliser, what does the ‘P’ stand for?

topics.title: Nutrition in Animals
topics.description: How animals obtain and process food — feeding modes and the human digestive system.

stories.sub: Every animal needs food — the methods vary wildly
stories.heading: Four ways animals get their food
list: Unlike plants, animals cannot make their own food — they are heterotrophic, feeding on other organisms.
A mosquito, a cow and a lion all eat completely differently, but each strategy solves the same problem.
Biologists group feeding methods into a handful of recognisable patterns.
stories.narration: Unlike plants, animals cannot make their own food — they are heterotrophic, feeding on other organisms. A mosquito, a cow and a lion all eat completely differently, but each strategy solves the same problem, and biologists group these into recognisable patterns.

stories.sub: Teeth tell a story
stories.heading: You can read an animal's diet from its mouth
list: A lion's sharp, pointed teeth are built for gripping and tearing flesh.
A cow's flat, ridged teeth are built for grinding tough plant fibre.
This is why comparing skulls and teeth is a classic way WAEC tests feeding adaptations.
stories.narration: A lion's sharp, pointed teeth are built for gripping and tearing flesh, while a cow's flat, ridged teeth are built for grinding tough plant fibre — comparing teeth like this is a classic way exams test feeding adaptations.

lessons.heading: Herbivores, carnivores, omnivores
list: Herbivores feed only on plants (e.g. cow, grasshopper, rabbit).
Carnivores feed only on other animals (e.g. lion, hawk).
Omnivores feed on both plants and animals (e.g. humans, pigs, chickens).
lessons.sub: Diet type = the first split in classifying feeding modes.
lessons.narration: Herbivores feed only on plants, like the cow and grasshopper. Carnivores feed only on other animals, like the lion and hawk. Omnivores, like humans and pigs, feed on both.

lessons.heading: Holozoic, parasitic and saprophytic feeding
list: Holozoic feeding: taking in solid, complex food and digesting it internally — how most animals (including humans) feed.
Parasitic feeding: an organism (parasite) lives on or in a host and feeds off it, often harming it (e.g. tapeworm).
Saprophytic feeding: feeding on dead and decaying organic matter by external digestion (mainly fungi and some bacteria, not typical animals).
lessons.sub: Holozoic = eat and digest inside. Parasitic = feed off a living host. Saprophytic = feed on the dead.
lessons.narration: Holozoic feeding means taking in solid food and digesting it internally, how most animals feed. Parasitic feeding means living on or in a host and feeding off it, like a tapeworm. Saprophytic feeding means feeding on dead matter by external digestion, mainly in fungi.

lessons.heading: Teeth and feeding adaptations
list: Carnivore teeth: sharp canines for gripping and tearing, and pointed molars for shearing flesh.
Herbivore teeth: broad, flat, ridged molars for grinding plant fibre; canines often reduced or absent.
A long gut (intestine) is typical of herbivores, since plant fibre is harder to digest and needs more processing time.
lessons.sub: Sharp teeth + short gut = carnivore. Flat teeth + long gut = herbivore.
lessons.narration: Carnivores have sharp canines for gripping and tearing, and pointed molars for shearing flesh. Herbivores have broad, flat, ridged molars for grinding plant fibre, and typically a longer gut, since plant fibre takes more processing time to digest.

lessons.heading: Two more specialised feeding methods
list: Filter feeders (e.g. some fish, baleen whales) strain tiny food particles out of large volumes of water.
Fluid feeders (e.g. mosquito, aphid, butterfly) use needle-like or tube-like mouthparts to feed on liquids like blood, sap or nectar.
Both are adaptations that avoid the need to chew solid food at all.
lessons.sub: Filter = strain solids from water. Fluid feeder = sip liquid through a tube.
lessons.narration: Filter feeders strain tiny food particles out of large volumes of water, like baleen whales. Fluid feeders use needle-like or tube-like mouthparts to feed on liquids such as blood, sap or nectar, like the mosquito and the butterfly.

lessons.heading: Matching mouthparts and gut length to diet
list: Sharp canines + short gut → carnivore. Flat grinding molars + long gut → herbivore.
Needle-like mouthparts (mosquito) → fluid feeder. Straining structures → filter feeder.
WAEC often shows a skull or mouthpart diagram and asks you to identify the feeding type.
lessons.sub: Match the tool to the job — teeth and mouthparts always match the diet.
lessons.narration: Sharp canines with a short gut mean a carnivore; flat grinding molars with a long gut mean a herbivore. Needle-like mouthparts mean a fluid feeder, and straining structures mean a filter feeder.

quiz.question: An animal that feeds only on other animals is called a
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — carnivores feed exclusively on other animals.
quiz.explainWrong: Feeding only on other animals defines a carnivore — herbivores eat only plants, omnivores eat both.
quiz.narration: An animal that feeds only on other animals is called a

stories.sub: Nine metres, several hours, one goal
stories.heading: What happens to your last meal
list: Food you swallow travels through roughly nine metres of digestive tract before what's left leaves your body.
Along the way, large food molecules are broken down into pieces small enough to enter your blood.
Every bite you eat is really a chemistry problem your gut has to solve.
stories.narration: Food you swallow travels through roughly nine metres of digestive tract before what's left leaves your body. Along the way, large food molecules are broken down into pieces small enough to enter your blood — every bite is really a chemistry problem your gut has to solve.

stories.sub: Why you can't just absorb a sandwich whole
stories.heading: The role of enzymes
list: Starch, protein and fat molecules are far too large to pass through the gut wall into the blood.
Digestive enzymes act like molecular scissors, cutting these large molecules into small, absorbable units.
Without enzymes, most of the food you eat would simply pass straight through you, unused.
stories.narration: Starch, protein and fat molecules are far too large to pass through the gut wall into the blood. Digestive enzymes act like molecular scissors, cutting these large molecules into small, absorbable units — without them, most food would simply pass through unused.

lessons.heading: What digestion means
list: Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed.
It happens in two ways: mechanical digestion (chewing, churning — physically breaking food into smaller pieces) and chemical digestion (enzymes breaking chemical bonds).
The alimentary canal is the tube food passes through, from mouth to anus.
lessons.sub: Mechanical = smaller pieces. Chemical = enzymes cutting molecules apart.
lessons.narration: Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed. It happens by mechanical digestion, like chewing, and chemical digestion, where enzymes break chemical bonds.

lessons.heading: Mouth → stomach → small intestine
list: Mouth: chewing (mechanical) plus salivary amylase begins starch digestion.
Stomach: churns food and adds acid and pepsin, which begins protein digestion.
Small intestine: bile (from the liver) emulsifies fat; pancreatic and intestinal enzymes complete digestion of starch, protein and fat.
lessons.sub: Starch starts in the mouth, protein starts in the stomach, fat digestion mainly happens in the small intestine.
lessons.narration: In the mouth, chewing and salivary amylase begin starch digestion. In the stomach, acid and pepsin begin protein digestion. In the small intestine, bile emulsifies fat, and pancreatic and intestinal enzymes complete digestion of starch, protein and fat.

lessons.heading: The small intestine — built to absorb
list: The inner wall of the small intestine is covered in finger-like projections called villi.
Villi hugely increase the surface area available for absorbing digested food into the blood.
Each villus has a rich blood supply to carry absorbed nutrients away quickly, keeping the concentration gradient steep.
lessons.sub: Villi = the small intestine's surface-area trick, just like root hairs for a plant.
lessons.narration: The inner wall of the small intestine is covered in finger-like projections called villi, which hugely increase the surface area for absorbing digested food. Each villus has a rich blood supply, carrying nutrients away quickly.

lessons.heading: What's left after absorption
list: The large intestine mainly absorbs water from the remaining undigested material.
This turns liquid waste into semi-solid faeces.
Faeces are stored in the rectum and expelled through the anus (egestion).
lessons.sub: Large intestine's job: reclaim water, not digest more food.
lessons.narration: The large intestine mainly absorbs water from the remaining undigested material, turning it into semi-solid faeces, which are stored in the rectum and expelled through the anus.

lessons.heading: Enzyme, substrate and product — the trio WAEC tests
list: Amylase breaks down starch into maltose (and further into glucose).
Protease (e.g. pepsin) breaks down protein into amino acids.
Lipase breaks down fat into fatty acids and glycerol.
lessons.sub: Amylase → starch. Protease → protein. Lipase → fat. Learn this table exactly.
lessons.narration: Amylase breaks down starch into maltose and glucose. Protease, like pepsin, breaks down protein into amino acids. Lipase breaks down fat into fatty acids and glycerol — a table WAEC tests directly and often.

quiz.question: Digestion is best defined as
options: the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble ones
the absorption of digested food into the blood
the removal of undigested waste from the body
the making of food by green plants
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — digestion breaks large insoluble molecules into small, soluble, absorbable ones.
quiz.explainWrong: Digestion is the breakdown step itself — absorption and egestion are separate, later processes.
quiz.narration: Digestion is best defined as

options: increase the surface area for absorption of digested food
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — villi greatly increase surface area for absorption, with a rich blood supply to carry nutrients away.
quiz.explainWrong: Villi's job is increasing surface area for absorption — acid production happens in the stomach, not here.
quiz.narration: Villi in the small intestine mainly function to

quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — protease (e.g. pepsin) breaks protein down into amino acids.
quiz.explainWrong: Protease digests protein into amino acids — amylase acts on starch, lipase acts on fat.
quiz.narration: Which enzyme breaks down protein into amino acids?

quiz.question: The main function of the large intestine is to
options: absorb water from undigested material, forming faeces
absorb digested food into the blood
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the large intestine's main job is reabsorbing water, turning waste into semi-solid faeces.
quiz.explainWrong: The large intestine mainly absorbs water — most digestion and nutrient absorption already happened in the small intestine.

topics.title: Transport Systems in Plants & Animals
topics.description: How plants move water and food through xylem and phloem, and how the circulatory system moves blood in animals.

stories.sub: No pump, no problem
stories.heading: How water climbs a 100-metre tree with no heart
list: Unlike animals, plants have no pump like a heart to push fluids around.
Yet giant trees move water from roots to leaves over 100 metres high.
The secret is a chain of physical forces: root pressure, capillarity, and most importantly, transpiration pull.
stories.narration: Unlike animals, plants have no pump like a heart to push fluids around, yet giant trees move water from roots to leaves over one hundred metres high. The secret is a chain of physical forces, most importantly transpiration pull.

stories.sub: A leaf sweats too
stories.heading: Why a tree can ‘drink’ hundreds of litres a day
list: A single large tree can lose hundreds of litres of water a day as vapour through its leaves.
This water loss, called transpiration, is mostly a side effect of gas exchange, not the main goal.
But the constant upward pull it creates is exactly what drags water up from the roots.
stories.narration: A single large tree can lose hundreds of litres of water a day as vapour through its leaves — a process called transpiration, mostly a side effect of gas exchange, but the constant upward pull it creates is what drags water up from the roots.

lessons.heading: Two transport tissues, two directions
list: Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals, in one direction only: upward, from roots to leaves.
Phloem transports food (mainly dissolved sugars), in both directions: from leaves (or storage organs) to wherever it's needed.
Together they form the plant's vascular system, running through roots, stems and leaves.
lessons.sub: Xylem: water, one-way, up. Phloem: food, both ways.
lessons.narration: Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals in one direction only, upward from roots to leaves. Phloem transports food in both directions, from leaves or storage organs to wherever it is needed.

lessons.heading: How xylem vessels are built for the job
list: Xylem vessels are made of dead cells joined end to end, forming continuous hollow tubes.
Their walls are strengthened with a waterproof substance called lignin.
Being dead and hollow removes any obstruction, letting water flow through easily under tension.
lessons.sub: Dead, hollow, lignified tubes — built purely for flow and strength, not living function.
lessons.narration: Xylem vessels are made of dead cells joined end to end into continuous hollow tubes, with walls strengthened by lignin. Being dead and hollow removes any obstruction, letting water flow through easily.

lessons.heading: The engine behind water movement
list: Water evaporates from cells inside the leaf and exits mainly through the stomata (transpiration).
This creates a slight suction that pulls more water up through the xylem to replace what was lost.
Water molecules stick to each other (cohesion), so the whole column of water in the xylem is pulled up together, like a drinking straw.
lessons.sub: Losing water at the top creates suction that pulls water up from the bottom.
lessons.narration: Water evaporates from leaf cells and exits mainly through the stomata, creating a slight suction that pulls more water up through the xylem. Because water molecules stick together, the whole column is pulled up together, like a drinking straw.

lessons.heading: What speeds up or slows down water loss
list: Higher temperature, lower humidity, and more wind all increase the rate of transpiration.
More light usually increases transpiration too, because stomata open wider in light for photosynthesis.
A waxy cuticle on the leaf surface reduces uncontrolled water loss.
lessons.sub: Hot, dry, windy, bright conditions all speed up transpiration.
lessons.narration: Higher temperature, lower humidity and more wind all increase the rate of transpiration, as does brighter light, since stomata open wider for photosynthesis. A waxy cuticle on the leaf surface helps reduce uncontrolled water loss.

lessons.heading: Xylem vs phloem — the comparison table
list: Xylem: dead cells, lignified walls, transports water/minerals, one direction (up).
Phloem: living cells, no lignin, transports dissolved food, both directions.
WAEC frequently asks you to identify a tissue from a description of just one or two of these features.
lessons.sub: Dead + lignin + water = xylem. Living + food + both ways = phloem.
lessons.narration: Xylem is made of dead, lignified cells transporting water and minerals upward only. Phloem is made of living cells with no lignin, transporting dissolved food in both directions — a comparison WAEC tests often.

quiz.question: Which tissue transports water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — xylem transports water and minerals upward from roots to leaves.
quiz.explainWrong: Xylem carries water and minerals upward — phloem carries food, and epidermis/cortex are not transport tissues.
quiz.narration: Which tissue transports water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots?

quiz.question: Xylem vessels are able to withstand tension partly because their walls are strengthened by
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — lignin strengthens and waterproofs xylem vessel walls.
quiz.explainWrong: Lignin is the strengthening substance in xylem walls — chlorophyll and chitin play no role here.
quiz.narration: Xylem vessels are able to withstand tension partly because their walls are strengthened by

quiz.question: The loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata, is called
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — transpiration is water loss as vapour, mainly through the stomata.
quiz.explainWrong: Water vapour loss through stomata is transpiration — translocation refers to food movement in phloem.
quiz.narration: The loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata, is called

quiz.question: Which condition would increase the rate of transpiration?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — heat and dry air both speed up water evaporation from the leaf.
quiz.explainWrong: High temperature and low humidity increase transpiration — darkness and still air would slow it down.
quiz.narration: Which condition would increase the rate of transpiration?

stories.sub: 100,000 km of pipes inside you
stories.heading: Your circulatory system, by the numbers
list: If you laid out all the blood vessels in an adult human end to end, they would stretch about 100,000 kilometres.
That's enough to circle the Earth roughly two and a half times.
The heart pumps blood through this entire network, once around roughly every minute at rest.
stories.narration: If you laid out all the blood vessels in an adult human end to end, they would stretch about one hundred thousand kilometres — enough to circle the Earth roughly two and a half times. The heart pumps blood through this whole network about once a minute at rest.

stories.sub: Why your heart has four chambers, not one
stories.heading: The double circulation advantage
list: Humans have a double circulatory system: blood passes through the heart twice on each full circuit.
One loop sends blood to the lungs for oxygen; the other loop sends oxygenated blood to the rest of the body.
This keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood mostly separate, so the body gets blood at full oxygen strength.
stories.narration: Humans have a double circulatory system: blood passes through the heart twice on each full circuit — once to the lungs for oxygen, and once to deliver that oxygenated blood to the rest of the body, keeping oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood mostly separate.

lessons.heading: What the circulatory system does
list: The circulatory system transports oxygen, digested food, hormones, and waste products around the body.
It consists of the heart (the pump), blood vessels (the pipes), and blood (the fluid carrying everything).
Humans have a closed double circulatory system: blood stays inside vessels and passes through the heart twice per circuit.
lessons.sub: Heart = pump. Vessels = pipes. Blood = delivery fluid.
lessons.narration: The circulatory system transports oxygen, digested food, hormones and waste around the body, using the heart as a pump, blood vessels as pipes, and blood as the fluid. Humans have a closed double circulatory system.

lessons.heading: Arteries, veins and capillaries
list: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, under high pressure, with thick, muscular, elastic walls.
Veins carry blood back to the heart, under low pressure, with thinner walls and valves to prevent backflow.
Capillaries are microscopic vessels, one cell thick, where actual exchange of substances with body tissues happens.
lessons.sub: Arteries away, veins back, capillaries where the real exchange happens.
lessons.narration: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, with thick, muscular walls. Veins carry blood back to the heart under low pressure, with valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries are microscopic, one cell thick, where exchange with tissues happens.

lessons.heading: Four chambers, one-way flow
list: The heart has four chambers: two upper atria (receive blood) and two lower ventricles (pump blood out).
The right side handles deoxygenated blood (to the lungs); the left side handles oxygenated blood (to the body).
One-way valves between chambers prevent blood from flowing backward.
lessons.sub: Right side = lungs. Left side = body. Valves keep flow one-way.
lessons.narration: The heart has four chambers: two atria that receive blood, and two ventricles that pump it out. The right side handles deoxygenated blood going to the lungs; the left side handles oxygenated blood going to the body, with valves keeping flow one-way.

lessons.heading: What's actually flowing through the pipes
list: Red blood cells carry oxygen, using the pigment haemoglobin.
White blood cells defend the body against infection.
Platelets help blood clot; plasma is the liquid part that carries dissolved substances like glucose, hormones and waste.
lessons.sub: Red cells carry oxygen, white cells fight germs, platelets clot, plasma carries everything dissolved.
lessons.narration: Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin. White blood cells defend against infection. Platelets help blood clot, and plasma, the liquid part, carries dissolved substances like glucose, hormones and waste.

lessons.heading: Artery vs vein — the quick test
list: Thick, muscular, elastic wall + no valves + carries blood away from heart → artery.
Thinner wall + valves present + carries blood toward heart → vein.

Exception to memorise: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood — the ‘artery/vein’ naming is about direction from the heart, not oxygen content.
lessons.sub: Artery vs vein is about direction (away/toward heart), NOT about oxygen content.
lessons.narration: A thick, muscular wall with no valves, carrying blood away from the heart, is an artery. A thinner wall with valves, carrying blood toward the heart, is a vein. Remember: the pulmonary artery and vein are the one exception where naming is about direction, not oxygen content.

quiz.question: Which blood vessel type carries blood away from the heart under high pressure?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — arteries carry blood away from the heart, with thick, muscular, elastic walls to handle high pressure.
quiz.explainWrong: Carrying blood away from the heart under high pressure is the artery's job — veins carry blood back, under low pressure.
quiz.narration: Which blood vessel type carries blood away from the heart under high pressure?

quiz.question: Exchange of substances between blood and body tissues happens mainly across the walls of the
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — capillaries are one cell thick, allowing efficient exchange with surrounding tissue.
quiz.explainWrong: Exchange happens at capillaries, which are thin enough for substances to pass through — arteries and veins are not.
quiz.narration: Exchange of substances between blood and body tissues happens mainly across the walls of the

quiz.question: Which side of the heart pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body?
options: Neither side — the lungs pump it
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — the left side of the heart handles oxygenated blood, pumping it out to the body.
quiz.explainWrong: The left side handles oxygenated blood to the body; the right side handles deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
quiz.narration: Which side of the heart pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body?

quiz.question: Which blood component is responsible for carrying oxygen around the body?
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — red blood cells carry oxygen bound to the pigment haemoglobin.
quiz.explainWrong: Oxygen transport is the job of red blood cells and haemoglobin — white blood cells fight infection, platelets clot blood.
quiz.narration: Which blood component is responsible for carrying oxygen around the body?

topics.title: Respiration & Gaseous Exchange
topics.description: How living things release energy from food, and how oxygen gets in while carbon dioxide gets out.

stories.sub: Two words, two very different processes
stories.heading: Respiration is not the same as breathing
list: Many students confuse ‘respiration’ with ‘breathing’ — but they are not the same process.
Breathing is the physical movement of air in and out of the lungs.
Respiration is the chemical release of energy from food, happening inside every living cell, all the time.
stories.narration: Many students confuse respiration with breathing, but they are not the same. Breathing is the physical movement of air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is the chemical release of energy from food, happening inside every living cell, all the time.

stories.sub: Why your muscles burn during a sprint
stories.heading: The body's emergency backup plan
list: During intense exercise, muscles can use oxygen faster than the blood can deliver it.
When this happens, cells switch briefly to anaerobic respiration, which doesn't need oxygen.
The lactic acid this produces is part of why muscles feel a burning fatigue during a hard sprint.
stories.narration: During intense exercise, muscles can use oxygen faster than the blood can deliver it. When this happens, cells switch briefly to anaerobic respiration, which doesn't need oxygen — the lactic acid it produces is part of why muscles feel a burning fatigue.

lessons.heading: What respiration actually is
list: Respiration is the chemical process that releases energy from food inside cells.
It happens continuously in every living cell, in both plants and animals, day and night.
The energy released powers every cell activity: movement, growth, repair, and more.
lessons.sub: Respiration = releasing usable energy from food, inside cells.
lessons.narration: Respiration is the chemical process that releases energy from food inside cells. It happens continuously, in every living cell, and the energy released powers every cell activity — movement, growth and repair.

lessons.heading: Respiration using oxygen
list: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to fully break down glucose, releasing a large amount of energy.
Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy).
This is the main type of respiration in most cells, most of the time.
lessons.sub: Aerobic = with oxygen = most energy released, most efficient.
lessons.narration: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to fully break down glucose, releasing a large amount of energy: glucose plus oxygen yields carbon dioxide, water and energy. This is the main type of respiration in most cells, most of the time.

lessons.heading: Respiration without oxygen
list: Anaerobic respiration releases energy from glucose without using oxygen — but releases far less energy per glucose molecule.
In humans, it produces lactic acid: glucose → lactic acid (+ energy).
In yeast (and some plants), it produces alcohol and carbon dioxide instead: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide (+ energy) — this is fermentation.
lessons.sub: Anaerobic = no oxygen = less energy = lactic acid (animals) or alcohol + CO2 (yeast).
lessons.narration: Anaerobic respiration releases energy from glucose without oxygen, but far less per glucose molecule. In humans it produces lactic acid; in yeast, it produces alcohol and carbon dioxide, a process called fermentation.

lessons.heading: Aerobic vs anaerobic, side by side
list: Aerobic: needs oxygen; products are CO2 and water; releases much more energy.
Anaerobic: no oxygen needed; products are lactic acid (animals) or alcohol + CO2 (yeast); releases much less energy.
Anaerobic respiration is a short-term backup, not a long-term substitute for aerobic respiration.
lessons.sub: Anaerobic buys time; aerobic does the real, efficient work.
lessons.narration: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water, releasing much more energy. Anaerobic respiration needs no oxygen but releases far less energy, and is only a short-term backup, not a long-term substitute.

lessons.heading: Uses of fermentation and common pitfalls
list: Fermentation by yeast is used industrially to make bread rise (CO2 bubbles) and to brew alcoholic drinks (ethanol).
Do not say plants only respire at night — plants respire all the time; they only photosynthesise in light.
Do not confuse respiration (releases energy, happens always) with photosynthesis (stores energy, needs light).
lessons.sub: Plants respire 24/7; they only photosynthesise when there's light.
lessons.narration: Fermentation by yeast is used industrially to make bread rise and to brew alcoholic drinks. Remember: plants respire all the time, not just at night — they only photosynthesise in light, and respiration and photosynthesis are not the same process.

the physical movement of air into and out of the lungs
the making of food using light energy

quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — respiration is the chemical release of energy from food inside living cells.
quiz.explainWrong: Respiration is the chemical energy release inside cells — moving air in and out of the lungs is breathing, a separate process.

quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — aerobic respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide, water and energy.
quiz.explainWrong: Aerobic respiration is glucose plus oxygen yielding carbon dioxide, water and energy — the other options describe photosynthesis or anaerobic respiration.

quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — human muscle cells produce lactic acid during anaerobic respiration when oxygen is insufficient.
quiz.explainWrong: Human cells produce lactic acid under anaerobic conditions — ethanol is the yeast product, not the human one.

options: releases much less energy from the same amount of glucose
releases much more energy from the same amount of glucose
requires oxygen just like aerobic respiration
only happens in plants, never in animals
quiz.explainCorrect: Correct — anaerobic respiration is far less efficient, releasing much less energy per glucose molecule.
quiz.explainWrong: Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy than aerobic respiration — it does not require oxygen, unlike aerobic.
